synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Yen Si-Yuan is eighteen, three weeks into adulthood and on her first lead role, when the production lawyer makes her read her morality clause aloud. Yang Pengcheng is twenty-five, from a family of judges and senior counsel, and the only person on the studio lot who doesn’t want anything from her. She decides he’s the most boring man she’s ever met. He keeps her pen.

His mother decides at breakfast that the actress is a logical match for no one. So begin three years of bowing at his family’s table while they talk past her, and he holds her hand under it and says nothing.

When his mother humiliates her in front of three hundred people, he says nothing again. She puts an ocean between them. For the first time in his life, Yang Pengcheng finds out what silence costs, and that it was never neutral.

Second chance · A lawyer who never raises his voice · She bows, until she doesn’t · Ongoing

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
This is the book in the series that hurts on purpose: a marriage gone cold, and a man who has to learn that staying silent is a choice, and never a neutral one.

The repair is slow and earned. You’ll see it in how he touches her. He falls asleep on her shoulder during script reads.

chapters.title: The Contract on Set
chapters.desc: Her first lead, at eighteen, and the production lawyer won’t let her sign until she’s read clause fourteen aloud. She asks if he’s always this boring. He keeps her pen.
chapters.content:
The first thing Yen Si-Yuan learned about being a leading actress was that nobody cared whether she could act until she’d signed about forty pages of paperwork. The second was that production lawyers were apparently born without the ability to smile.

At least, the one across the desk from her seemed to have been.

“Page seventeen.”

She looked down at the document, and at the man, and back at the document. “Again?”

“Yes.”

“I’ve read page seventeen.”

“You skimmed page seventeen.”

“I read it with my eyes.”

“That’s generally how reading works,” said the man, without looking up.

It was Monday the third of January 2022, the first morning of the shoot, in a temporary production office on the studio lot with a strip light that ticked and a window onto the car park. He was squaring the edges of a stack of papers with long fingers and an unnecessary degree of precision. White shirt, charcoal suit, a tie loosened a quarter of an inch, like a man who’d been working since seven and had allowed himself exactly that much. An understated watch. Neat hair. The face of a man who’d never once been late for anything.

Yang Pengcheng. Twenty-five. Production counsel, on loan to the film from his family’s chambers, and according to the assistant director who’d walked her over, particular about contracts.

She’d been warned. The assistant director, a tired woman called Fong with a headset round her neck and three phones, had walked her across the lot at nine with a hand on her elbow, talking the whole way. He’s from the Yang chambers. You know the Yangs. Old family, all of them lawyers, the grandfather was a chief justice. The studio borrows him for the big contracts because nobody’s ever got a clause past him. He made our male lead read his indemnity twice. Don’t argue with him. Don’t be charming at him either, it doesn’t work, we’ve tried. Just read what he gives you, sign where he points, and you’ll be out by eleven. At the door Fong had looked at her, all eighteen years and three weeks of her, in her good coat with the pen her sisters had given her in the pocket, and added, more kindly, He’s not unkind. He’s just thorough. Thorough is rare round here. You’ll be glad of it one day.

It was now a quarter to twelve. She hadn’t expected this particular degree of thoroughness.

“Mr. Yang. Do you intend to make me memorise the whole contract?”

“If necessary.” He looked up at last, and his face did nothing at all. “Page seventeen, Miss Yen.”

She pressed her lips together. She’d turned eighteen three weeks ago. She’d spent the autumn in acting workshops and screen tests and costume fittings, learning to cry on cue and hit a mark without looking down and say the same line twenty times without losing what was under it. She’d also learned that adults liked telling young actresses to be grateful. She was grateful. This was her first lead: a real film, a director people had heard of, a budget, and a cast with three actors she’d grown up watching. She had no intention of losing it over paperwork.

Still.

“Do you make every actress read her contract aloud?”

“Only the ones who look determined to sign without understanding it.” He turned a page and put one finger beside a heading. “Clause fourteen. Start there.”

14. MORALITY AND PUBLIC CONDUCT.

Oh. That one. The production coordinator had called it standard: something about the production’s reputation, and not getting into trouble during filming. She’d assumed it was straightforward. Mr. Yang apparently didn’t.

“The whole clause,” he said.

She took a breath. “The Artist agrees to conduct herself in a manner consistent with the professional standards and public image reasonably expected of the production—”

“Go on.”

“The Artist shall not knowingly engage in conduct that materially damages the reputation of the Production Company, the film, its investors or affiliated commercial partners—”

“Stop there.” He leaned back a fraction. “What does materially damages mean to you?”

“Something that does actual damage.”

“That’s vague.”

“Something that does actual, significant damage.”

“Better. What makes it significant?”

She stared at him. He stared back. The air conditioner hummed.

“Mr. Yang. I think you’re asking me to do your job.”

“I’m asking you to understand what you’re signing,” he said, so calmly that she couldn’t find a proper reason to be offended, and so she looked down and read on.

The clause went on longer than she’d expected: public statements, undisclosed endorsements, conflicts of interest, conduct at publicity events, the circumstances in which the company could serve her a formal notice. When she reached the end he asked her the difference between a material breach and a minor one. She answered. He corrected part of it. She argued with another part. He listened all the way through, which surprised her, and then explained why her reading was incomplete, which didn’t. She argued again. It took six more minutes.

At last he closed the file. “All right.”

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

She smiled at him. He didn’t smile back, and her smile went slowly out like a light on a timer. “Are we finished?”

“With the morality clause.”

“There’s more?”

“Several pages.”

She leaned back in her chair and wondered, for the first time that morning, whether saying yes to this film had been a terrible mistake.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside, the set was much louder. Technicians went past the glass with equipment cases. Wardrobe assistants carried garment bags down the corridor. Somebody was shouting about a missing lighting clamp, and a runner went by with three coffees balanced in one hand. Through the window she could see her leading man at the entrance to the soundstage, laughing with the director, and she was supposed to meet him at a table read that afternoon. Instead she was trapped with a man who believed every sentence in a contract deserved a public performance.

“Page twenty-three.”

“Mr. Yang. Can I ask you something? Do you enjoy this?”

He paused. “Enjoy what?”

“Contracts.”

“Not especially.”

“Then why do you look so happy doing it?”

For the first time something nearly moved in his face. His eyes came up to hers. “I don’t.”

She laughed. It got out before she could stop it, loud in the small office, and he watched her do it for a second before he looked back at the page.

“Page twenty-three, Miss Yen.”

“You’re really something.”

“I’ve been told.”

“Not in a good way, I imagine.”

“Usually not,” said Yang Pengcheng, and she laughed again.

He passed her a pen to initial with. It was her own, which she’d put down on his desk when she arrived: a black fountain pen with a silver clip, heavier than the disposable ones the assistants carried, a present from her sisters for the first day. She signed where he pointed, one page and the next and the next, in her round hand with the last stroke of her surname running on a little further than it needed to. He checked every one. Not quickly, and not carelessly. He checked the dates and the initials and the schedules attached, and asked her to confirm the spelling of her legal name and the bank details on the payment form.

At the last page he put his finger beside the signature line. “Read the declaration first.”

She read it, and signed, and pushed the whole stack back across the desk. “Of course. There.”

He went through it once more and slid it into a folder.

She managed to sit still for about three seconds. “Mr. Yang? Are you always this boring?”

She asked it with such real curiosity that he took a moment to answer. “At work?”

“Generally.”

“Probably.”

“That’s unfortunate. You’re young. Twenty-five, the assistant director said. You’re only seven years older than me.”

“Seven years and two months.”

“That’s still young.”

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome,” said Si-Yuan, with her chin in her hand.

There was something ridiculous about how composed he was. He didn’t fidget, or interrupt, or seem to mind a silence. Most people filled silences because they couldn’t stand them. Yang Pengcheng appeared to regard silence as a perfectly acceptable form of conversation. She’d never in her life been able to leave a quiet room quiet.

“Have you got a girlfriend?”

His hand stopped above the briefcase. “Why?”

“I’m curious.”

“That isn’t a reason.”

“You’re right. It’s a feeling.”

“Then I’m afraid I don’t see what it has to do with the contract.”

“You’re very difficult to talk to.”

“That isn’t a contractual matter either,” he said, and she stared at him, and laughed so loudly that someone in the corridor looked in through the glass.

For a man who barely smiled, he was unfairly good at making her laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time they finished the morning had gone, and the light across the lot had moved to the other side of the cars. He stood and buttoned his jacket and picked up his briefcase.

“Thank you for going through everything with me.”

It was the first thing he’d said all morning that sounded like a person and not a clause.

“Thank you for not letting me sign something I didn’t understand.” Then, because it seemed important, she held out her hand. “Yen Si-Yuan.”

He looked at her hand, and at her, and a faint line appeared between his eyebrows. “We’ve been introduced.”

“I know. I’m doing it properly this time.”

He considered whether she meant it. Then he took her hand, once, firmly. “Yang Pengcheng. Production counsel.”

“Actress.”

“I know.”

“Then we’re acquainted.”

“Apparently,” he said, and let go.

That should have been the end of it: a routine morning between a new actress and the lawyer assigned to her film. But when she turned to collect her bag he glanced down at the desk, where her pen was still lying beside the folder.

“Miss Yen. Is this yours?”

She checked her bag, and then the desk. “Oh. Yes. Thank you.”

He looked at the pen in his hand for a second longer than he needed to. Then, instead of giving it back, he put it into the inside pocket of his jacket.

“Mr. Yang? My pen.”

“I’ll keep it. I’ll return it through production.”

“Why?”

“You’ll need it for the next round of paperwork.”

“I’ve got other pens.”

“I’m sure.”

“Then why are you keeping that one?”

“Because you left it on my desk,” said Yang Pengcheng.

She opened her mouth, and shut it, and narrowed her eyes. “That’s stealing.”

“That’s safekeeping.”

“There’s a difference?”

“Legally, yes.”

She looked at him, and shook her head, and laughed. “You’re a very strange person, Mr. Yang.”

“I’ve been told.” He opened the office door. “Your table read is at three. You should eat something first.”

She went a few steps down the corridor and turned round. He was still standing in the doorway.

“Mr. Yang? Don’t lose my pen.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise?”

A short pause. “Yes.”

She went off down the corridor into the noise of the production floor, satisfied.

He stood where he was a while longer, in the quiet office. Then he took the pen out of his pocket. A small silver engraving ran along its side, in three initials: Y.S.Y. He looked at them, and put the pen back, and shut the door.

There were three contracts waiting for him, a location agreement to amend before the evening shoot, and a conference call with the production company’s senior counsel at four. He had no reason to remember an actress who’d spent most of a morning arguing with him over a document she’d meant to sign in five minutes. He went back to his desk and opened his briefcase and put the pen, carefully, in the inner pocket where he kept things he meant to keep.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the way to the table read she sat on an apple box behind the soundstage with a bun from craft services and typed with one thumb.

Si-Yuan: The lawyer made me read my contract OUT LOUD.

Si-Jie (Questions): All of it?? How long? Was he old? Was he mean? Did you cry? Are you allowed to tell us what’s in it?

Si-Yuan: Three hours. Twenty-five. Not mean. Boring. No. No.

Si-Jie (Questions): Twenty-five isn’t boring, twenty-five is a demographic

Si-Jie (Questions): Is he handsome? Be honest. Scale of one to the male lead

Si-Yuan: That’s not a relevant question. He’d say that’s not a relevant question. He says things like that.

Si-Jie (Questions): That’s a yes

Si-Yuan: It’s a no. He’s very neat. He squares paper. He’s got a watch that tells the time and nothing else.

Si-Jie (Questions): You looked at his WATCH

Si-Yuan: He kept my pen.

There was a pause long enough for her to finish the bun.

Si-Wei (Watching): The pen we gave you?

Si-Yuan: He says it’s safekeeping. Legally.

Si-Wei (Watching): Did you ask for it back?

Si-Yuan: Twice.

Si-Wei (Watching): And he still has it.

Si-Yuan: He says he’ll return it through production.

Si-Wei (Watching): He won’t.

Si-Jie (Questions): SI-WEI WHAT DOES THAT MEAN

Si-Wei (Watching): It means she’s going to have to go and get it.

Si-Yuan put the phone on her knee and looked across the car park at the production office, where the blind in the end window was half down and a man in a charcoal suit was on the phone with his back to the glass, and decided that he was the most boring man she had ever met, and that she’d go and get her pen on Thursday. She put Thursday: pen into her calendar, and deleted it, because that was ridiculous, and then put it in again, because it was her pen.

chapters.title: A Logical Match
chapters.desc: His mother rules at breakfast that the actress is a logical match for no one. That night he waits for her at a noodle stall by the studio gate; at four in the morning, in costume, she kisses him first. The first time she calls him Pengcheng.
chapters.epigraph: “That girl is a logical match for no one.”
chapters.content:
The first time Yang Pengcheng mentioned a woman at breakfast, his mother didn’t ask whether she was beautiful. She asked whether the woman had a degree. The second question was whether she came from a respectable family, and the third was whether she meant to go on working after she married.

He answered that the woman in question was an actress, and his mother put her teacup down. Not loudly. She’d never needed to.

“An actress. Which family?”

“Yen.”

“The Yen family? Property?”

“And media.”

“I know what they do.”

“Then I don’t need to explain it,” said Pengcheng, and went on eating.

It was Friday the eighteenth of February 2022, and his mother was dressed for chambers at seven in the morning: cream silk blouse, pearl earrings, hair pinned flat behind her head. At sixty she carried the authority of a woman who’d spent forty years in courtrooms and boardrooms and had grown used to people rethinking their arguments when she raised an eyebrow. Senior counsel. Head of the family chambers. And, in her own estimation, the person best qualified to decide whether her only son was making a sensible choice.

“How old is she?”

“Eighteen.”

Her face changed. “Pengcheng. She’s a child.”

He put his chopsticks down. “She’s an adult. She’s working. She’s financially independent of her family, and perfectly capable of making decisions about her own career.”

“That isn’t what I asked.” She reached for her tea. “An actress. Eighteen years old. No legal education. No idea what our family is, or what is expected of the person who stands beside you. Your father and I have spent our lives building something.”

“Someone who can stand beside me.”

“Someone who understands the position.”

“Those aren’t mutually exclusive.”

His mother looked at him across the breakfast table, and then she said it with the flat finality of a judgment being handed down.

“That girl is a logical match for no one.”

He drank some tea. “That’s a broad conclusion.”

“Don’t be clever. You’re twenty-five. You’ve your own practice to establish, your father’s clients to keep, and an obligation to this family. You can’t afford to tangle yourself up with someone whose whole life is cameras.”

“She’s a person, Mother. Not a risk assessment.”

The housekeeper came in to clear the plates, and neither of them said anything until she’d gone. Then his mother straightened her napkin.

“I hope you’re not serious about her.”

He looked at his watch. “I have a meeting. Good morning, Mother.”

He left before she could ask him anything else. In the car he sat for a minute with the engine off and his hands on the wheel, and found he couldn’t have told her whether he was serious, because he hadn’t let himself ask. He’d only noticed that he’d said eighteen in the tone he used for a fact he intended to defend.

✦ ✦ ✦

He still had her pen.

She’d come to the production office for it three times in seven weeks: the Thursday after the contract, a Tuesday in January with a question about her overseas schedule, and the week before, about an amendment that could have been an email. Each time she’d sat on the corner of the chair across his desk and argued with him about something, and each time she’d gone away again without asking for it, and both of them knew exactly why.

At 11:43 that night her name came up on his phone. In his contacts it still said Miss Yen (Page Seventeen), because he’d typed it on the first day and hadn’t changed it.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Are you awake?

He was in his office at the chambers with a location agreement for an overseas shoot open in front of him.

Pengcheng: Yes.

The dots came and went.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): I have a legal question. If someone accidentally eats the prop cake during filming, is that destruction of production property?

He looked at the screen.

Pengcheng: Was it an accident?

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): I was hungry.

Pengcheng: Was it a prop?

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): It was supposed to be. It was a very realistic cake.

Pengcheng: Then I’d advise you not to tell the production manager.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): You’re a lawyer. Aren’t you supposed to tell me what the law says?

Pengcheng: I’m telling you what I’d advise my client. My client should eat dinner.

She sent a photograph: herself on an apple box beside the set, still in costume, hair in elaborate period curls, a streak of make-up along her jaw, a paper cup of water on the floor beside her. She was holding up two fingers.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Dinner.

He looked at the photograph for longer than he needed to, and rang her.

“Is that what you’re calling dinner?”

She laughed down the phone. “You’re very judgemental.”

“It’s nearly midnight.”

“We’ve been shooting since four. We ate at five.”

“That’s seven hours.”

“You’re counting?”

“Somebody should.” He leaned back in his chair. “How long have you got left?”

“One more scene. Maybe two hours.”

“Maybe?”

“Film doesn’t work in exact times, Mr. Yang.”

“I’m aware. I’m asking because I’m deciding whether to wait for you.”

The line went quiet. He looked at the location agreement on his desk. He hadn’t decided anything. He’d found himself asking.

“Wait for me?”

“There’s a noodle stall by the studio gate. It’s open late.”

“You’re inviting me to eat? At two in the morning?”

“Unless you’d prefer to wait for breakfast.”

“You’re strange.”

“So you’ve mentioned.”

“All right. I’ll come.”

“Eat properly before you go back to work tomorrow.”

“Yes, Dad,” said Si-Yuan, and he shut his eyes.

“Don’t call me that.”

She was still laughing when the call ended.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got to the studio a little before two, in dark trousers and a white shirt with the sleeves rolled to the forearm, his jacket thrown over the passenger seat. He’d spent the last hour finishing the location agreement and another twenty minutes arguing with a production executive about an indemnity. He was tired. He was beginning to suspect he’d made a mistake.

The stall sat outside the gate under a faded red awning, with four plastic tables on the pavement and a television muttering behind the counter. He ordered two bowls of beef noodles and sat down to wait.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Coming out.

He almost didn’t recognise her. She hadn’t changed out of costume. She came through the gate in a pale blue period dress with embroidered sleeves and her hair still up in its pins and ornaments, with a long piece of it falling over one shoulder, her make-up intact, her mouth a muted rose. She was carrying a pair of white trainers in one hand. On her feet were a pair of plastic house slippers.

He looked at her feet. She followed his eyes.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face has. My character wears embroidered shoes. They’re agony. Somebody in wardrobe lent me these.” She put the trainers down by the table and looked at the two bowls. Her face lit up. “You ordered? How did you know what I have?”

“I asked the owner. I told him you were coming.”

Her expression went soft. It was such a small thing, a bowl of noodles and a question asked of a man behind a counter, and she looked at him like he’d done something much larger. He pulled out the chair opposite.

“Sit. It’ll go cold.”

She sat, and picked up her chopsticks, and took one mouthful and shut her eyes. “Oh.”

“Then eat,” he said, and she did, and for the first few minutes she was too hungry to talk, and he found he didn’t mind. The studio was still awake behind them; a crew member went through the gate with a light stand, and a production assistant hurried past with a clipboard. The air smelled of rain coming, fried garlic, broth.

When she’d slowed down she put her elbows on the table. “The director said I was too polite today.”

“Too polite?”

“My character’s supposed to hate the male lead. And apparently I keep smiling at him.”

“And do you smile at him?”

“No! I was acting.”

“Then perhaps try looking less pleased to see him.”

She stared at him. “Are you making fun of me?”

“A little.”

“You’re different outside the office.”

“How?”

“You’re still boring. But slightly less boring.”

“That’s generous.”

“I know,” said Si-Yuan, and went back to her noodles.

She told him about the shoot: the director who changed lines at the last minute, the leading man who couldn’t find his mark, a hair ornament that wardrobe had lost twice in one week. He listened. He asked questions, and not the kind people ask while waiting for their turn. When she mentioned a scene she’d struggled with, he asked whether they’d reshot it. When she complained about the night schedule, he asked whether the revised shooting plan had accounted properly for rest periods. When she said the assistant director was trying to bring an overseas location forward, he asked whether the permit applications had gone in.

She put her chopsticks down. “Can you stop being a lawyer for five minutes?”

“I’m eating.”

“You’re interrogating me. About permits.”

He considered it, and nodded. “All right.” A few seconds went by. “How was your scene today? The hard one.”

She blinked. “It was better. The director said I’d finally understood what he wanted.”

“Then you did well.”

Her fingers stopped. She was used to compliments that came with conditions. You look pretty. You were good today. You’re lucky to have this chance. He’d said it like it was a plain fact, and didn’t need decorating.

“Thank you,” she said.

He looked at his watch. “Eat a bit more. I’ll drive you back.”

“Haven’t you got work tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

“Then why are you here?”

He didn’t answer straight away. “You said you were hungry.”

It was a ridiculous answer, almost painfully simple, and it was the kindest thing anyone had done for her all week. She looked down at her bowl before he could see her face. He saw it anyway, and didn’t mention it.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly four when he parked by the production entrance. She’d talked most of the way, about her next scene, an actress she admired, a haircut she wanted for her next part, and then somewhere along the way she’d gone quiet, with one leg folded under her and the costume gathered round her knees.

“Sleepy?”

“A little.”

“Sleep when you get home. Don’t go over your scenes till dawn.”

She turned her head. “How do you know I do that?”

“You told me last week.”

He stopped the car with the engine still running. The security lights made pale circles on the empty car park. She had a long day ahead, sore feet, hairpins pulling at her scalp, and she’d have to be back in make-up before noon, and she didn’t want to get out.

“Mr. Yang? Why do you keep coming to see me?”

He turned towards her. She wasn’t smiling or teasing. She was waiting.

“I don’t think I’ve been coming very often.”

“You came last week.”

“You had a contract amendment.”

“And the week before.”

“Your overseas schedule.”

“And tonight.”

“You were hungry.”

She gave him a small look. “You’re very good at finding reasons. Have you got someone? A girlfriend? You never answered.”

“No.”

“Do you want one?”

He looked at her. “That’s a personal question.”

“You can answer or not.”

“Then I’ll think about it.”

“You’re avoiding it,” she said, smiling, and then the smile went, and she leaned towards him across the car, and he saw her move and didn’t understand what she meant by it until she’d done it.

“Si-Yuan—”

She kissed him. It was quick and a little clumsy and her mouth was warm and tasted of the broth. For one suspended second he didn’t move at all. She pulled back with her eyes wide, like she hadn’t really expected to do it, or had, and was now looking at him with a mixture of embarrassment and determination that he found hard to look away from.

“Sorry.”

“Why are you apologising?”

“Because I kissed you.”

“I noticed.” He watched her go pink. “Did you want to?”

She nodded.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

He let out a long breath. He lifted one hand and stopped it just short of her cheek. “May I?”

She looked at his hand, and at him, and nodded, and his fingers settled on her jaw, and this time he kissed her. He did it without any hurry and without the surprise of someone caught out. He kissed her with a restraint that made her more aware of him than anything else could have: the warmth of his hand, his thumb near her cheekbone, the careful way he tipped his head to meet her. When he drew back she was still close, with her eyes slowly opening.

“You’re going to have trouble with that lipstick,” he said.

She stared at him and burst out laughing. “That’s what you’re thinking about?”

“Among other things.”

He took a tissue from the console and gave it to her. She held it and looked at him over it.

“You’re not going to tell me I shouldn’t have done that?”

“Do you regret it?”

“No.”

“Then I don’t see the point.” He watched her lower the tissue. Her smile had gone smaller and less sure. “Ask what you want to ask.”

“Do you like me?”

He spent his days choosing words for a living, and understood better than most men his age what a careless sentence could cost. He found he didn’t want to give her a convenient one.

“I like spending time with you. I like talking to you, even when you’re difficult. And I wanted to kiss you just now.”

The corners of her mouth went up. “That’s better.”

She reached across the console and took his hand, and slid her fingers between his, and he let them stay there. A security guard walked past the car without looking. Somewhere inside the building someone would be printing the next day’s call sheet.

Eventually he said it. “You should go. You’ve got a call time.”

“You’re so romantic.”

“I’ve been told. By no one.”

She laughed, and leaned across and kissed his cheek, and opened the door and gathered up her dress and her trainers. Then she bent down and looked back in at him.

“Pengcheng.”

It was the first time she’d called him that. He went still.

“Next time, don’t make me eat alone.”

“I won’t.”

She smiled and shut the door. He watched her cross the car park in borrowed slippers that made no sound at all, and at the entrance she turned round and lifted her hand, and he lifted his.

His phone went before he’d put the car in gear.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): I forgot to tell you something. I think I like you.

He typed something, and deleted it, and typed again.

Pengcheng: I know.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Yang Pengcheng. You’re so annoying.

Pengcheng: Go to sleep, Si-Yuan.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Goodnight ❤️

He put the phone down and sat with his hands on the wheel in the empty car park at four in the morning, with an unfinished brief at home and a mother who’d spent breakfast explaining why an actress could never be a sensible match for him. For the first time that day he wasn’t thinking about any of it. He was thinking about a girl in a period costume who’d kissed him in a car park and then told him he wasn’t romantic enough.

He started the engine, and drove home with her pen still in his inside pocket.

chapters.title: Secret
chapters.desc: A secret the whole set has guessed. She calls him her boyfriend by accident; he says he doesn’t object. The first night at his flat, explicit: she leads, he doesn’t say a word. He renegotiates her contract without telling her.
chapters.epigraph: “Your heart’s very loud for a man who never says anything.”
chapters.content:
By March the hair and make-up department had reached a collective understanding that Yen Si-Yuan was a terrible liar. It wasn’t that she was bad at it in general. She was charming and quick and could look anyone in the eye while saying something demonstrably untrue. The problem was Yang Pengcheng, or, more exactly, her face whenever his name came up.

The make-up artist leaned in with the eyeliner. “Don’t move. Your boyfriend’s here.”

Si-Yuan’s eyes went wide in the mirror. “What?”

“Don’t look.”

“I wasn’t looking.”

“You’re looking now. And your face is going red.”

Across the trailer the wardrobe assistant made a small, suspiciously delighted noise. “Is it the lawyer? The one who doesn’t smile?”

“He’s not my boyfriend.”

“Then the man who’s been standing outside your trailer for twenty minutes is here to discuss your tax return,” said the make-up artist.

“He smiles,” said Si-Yuan, before she could stop herself.

Both women went quiet. The make-up artist turned round slowly with the brush in her hand. “Oh?”

The trailer erupted.

✦ ✦ ✦

It had started with small things. A coffee left on the step of her trailer before a dawn call. A familiar car near the studio gate at the end of a night shoot. A phone call that went on for eleven minutes when neither of them had anything to say. He never stayed long; he had his own work and clients and a schedule far less forgiving than hers. But he turned up. Sometimes to review a production document, sometimes to see the director about an amendment, sometimes because he’d finished a meeting nearby, and sometimes, she suspected, because he’d invented a reason. She’d never asked. She liked having him around too much to spoil it by asking.

The make-up artist noticed first, and wardrobe second, and third was the assistant director, Fong, who caught Pengcheng holding Si-Yuan’s handbag while she turned out her pockets looking for her phone, and walked away without a word and with an expression of enormous private satisfaction. By the third week of March the crew had come to an unspoken conclusion: the two of them were together, and hadn’t been told.

When she got out of the chair he was standing at the bottom of the trailer steps in a navy suit, reading something on his phone, with a folder under his arm.

“Finished?”

“I’ve got fifteen minutes.”

He looked at his watch. “Then you should eat.”

“Hello to you too. How was your day? Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Lunch.”

She was triumphant. “Lunch isn’t a food. You do it too.”

He gave her a look, and took a container out of a paper bag on the step beside him. “Egg sandwich. You said yesterday the catering was terrible and you didn’t eat much.”

“You brought me food? Did you make it?”

“The café downstairs made it.”

“Oh.”

“Disappointed?”

She considered lying. “Maybe.”

His mouth moved. It wasn’t quite a smile, but it was close enough, and she pointed at him with the sandwich. “There. You did it. You smiled.”

“I didn’t. Eat your sandwich.”

She laughed, and behind the trailer a wardrobe assistant took a photograph of the two of them for the group chat.

✦ ✦ ✦

Late that night she was sitting on an equipment case in an empty production office, watching him work on his laptop. She’d followed him there on the pretext of returning a phone charger she didn’t have. He knew she didn’t have one. Neither of them had mentioned it.

“You’re staring,” he said, without looking up.

“I’m observing. Staring’s rude. Observing’s professional.” She leaned forward. “What are you doing?”

“Reviewing an amendment. To your contract.”

“My contract? What about it?”

“Nothing you need to worry about.”

She reached over and touched his sleeve. “Pengcheng. Look at me.”

He stopped typing and turned. She smiled at him. “Hi.”

He looked at her for a second, and closed the laptop halfway. “Hello.”

“You’re very easy to distract.”

“You’re very persistent.”

She took his hand. Her nails were painted a pale pink that had started to chip at the edges, and he looked down at them.

“Your polish is coming off.”

“That’s because I’ve been working. You could fix it for me. You’re my boyfriend. You’re supposed to be useful.”

The word came out so easily that neither of them reacted for a second. Then she blinked, and he looked at her, and she found the floor interesting.

“I mean—”

“Your boyfriend,” he said.

“Unless you object.”

He didn’t answer. Then he turned his hand over under hers and laced their fingers together. “I don’t.”

Her smile came slowly. “Does that mean you’re officially responsible for my nail polish?”

“Among other things. Such as?”

“Buying me food. Driving me home. Answering my calls. Being nice to me.”

“That last one might need some discussion,” said Pengcheng, and she gasped, and he smiled, and this time she was certain of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly midnight when he drove her back to his flat, and she was asleep against the window before they’d crossed the harbour. At a red light he reached over and moved a strand of hair off her face, and she opened one eye.

“You’re still here.”

“Where else would I be?”

His flat was quiet and tidy. The first time she’d come, she’d spent fifteen minutes going along his bookshelves. The second time, she’d complained that his fridge held nothing but water, milk and an unreasonable number of eggs. Tonight she walked in without asking where anything was, left her shoes by the door and her bag on the sofa, and went straight to the kitchen.

“You ate on the way.”

“That was three hours ago.”

He opened the fridge. There was rice, vegetables, cold chicken, a container of soup. She looked over his shoulder. “You’ve got food. You told me you only had eggs.”

“I also have other things. You didn’t ask.”

He moved round the kitchen with the same economy he had at work: rice into the cooker, soup into a pan, a plate from the cupboard. She sat on a stool and watched him.

“You can cook. You look like somebody who’d pay someone to do everything.”

“I can do things myself.”

“I know. That’s why I like you,” she said, and his hand paused on the spoon and then went on stirring.

They ate at the counter. She told him about the evening’s scene, and he asked whether she was satisfied with it, and whether the director agreed. Then she told him about the make-up artist.

He put his spoon down. “She knows?”

“Everybody knows. Hair. Make-up. Wardrobe. Fong, probably. Apparently I’m terrible at hiding things.”

“That’s a lot of people.” He was quiet. “Be careful. You’re an actress. People talk, and not all of them kindly.”

“Are you ashamed of me?”

His eyes came up at once. “No.” It was so fast she blinked. “People make stories out of private lives. I don’t want your work touched by something that has nothing to do with your performance.”

She looked at him, and nodded, and couldn’t leave a serious moment alone for long. “Besides, everyone already thinks you’re my boyfriend.”

“That’s because I am,” he said, and went on eating.

She stared at him. Then she put her spoon down and got off the stool and came round the counter, and stood between his knees, and took his face in her hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

She led. He’d wondered, in the weeks of coffees and car parks, whether she would, and she did, without asking him anything except, at his bedroom door, with her hand flat on his chest:

“Is this all right?”

“Yes.”

“You’re very calm.”

“I’m not calm,” said Pengcheng, and it was the most honest thing she’d ever heard him say.

She undid his tie and pulled it out from under his collar. She undid his shirt, button by button, and he stood still and let her, watching her face and not her hands, and when the shirt was open she put her palms flat on his chest and felt his heart going hard and fast under them, which nothing in his face had told her. She looked up at him in surprise. He looked back, and said nothing, and let her see it.

He undressed her like he’d be examined on it. The zip at the back of her dress, slowly, all the way down. The straps off her shoulders, one at a time. The dress down to the floor, and he held her hand while she stepped out of it. He was precise about everything and he didn’t speak. He kissed her shoulder where the strap had been, and the side of her neck, and the place under her ear that made her catch her breath, and he noticed that, and did it again, and filed it away. She could see him filing it away. It made her laugh, shakily, against his mouth.

“You’re taking notes.”

“Yes.”

He laid her down on his tidy bed and looked at her in the light from the hall, and then he learned her the way he read a contract: every line, in order, nothing skimmed. His mouth on her breast, slow, until she arched into it. His hand down her stomach, and between her thighs, slow and certain, watching her face the whole time for what each thing did, adjusting. When she said his name he stopped and looked at her.

“Don’t stop. Keep going. Exactly that.”

He kept going exactly that, and she came apart under his hand with her fingers in his hair and her eyes shut, much faster than she’d meant to, and lay there breathing, astonished, while he waited.

“Again,” she said, when she could.

“Are you sure?”

“Pengcheng. Get undressed.”

He did, and she watched him do it, and he let her watch. She pulled him down and he came into her slowly, all the way, and stopped, and held himself there over her on his forearms, still not saying anything, looking at her like she was the only clause in the world that mattered. She wrapped her legs round him. He moved slowly, then less slowly when she asked him to, with his face close to hers and his breathing ragged and his mouth shut tight on whatever he wasn’t saying, and when she came the second time she held on to him and said his name out loud into the quiet of his flat, and a moment later he followed her with a sound she’d never heard him make, low and broken, into her hair.

Afterwards she lay on his chest with his heart going slower under her ear.

“You didn’t say anything. The whole time,” she said.

“No.”

“Not one word.”

“I was paying attention.” His hand moved once on her back. “Did you mind?”

She thought about it. “No. I could hear it anyway.” She lifted her head. “Your heart’s very loud for a man who never says anything.”

He looked at the ceiling. “Don’t tell anyone.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was one thing he didn’t tell her.

Two days later a revised version of her talent agreement went round between the production company, her agency and the lawyers. The changes were substantial. Her fee schedule had been revised. Her promotional obligations were defined more tightly. The company’s rights over her image had been narrowed. The termination clause now required written notice and a proper chance to respond. There were new protections around schedule changes and overseas filming.

It was a better contract by a long way. Pengcheng had negotiated every line of it over four days with the production company’s senior legal team, carefully. Every amendment had a contractual or commercial reason behind it. Nothing had been added because she was his girlfriend, or so he told himself. He hadn’t told her. He hadn’t asked whether she wanted it. He hadn’t mentioned that the original had clauses that would turn against her as her profile grew. He’d had it put right.

On Sunday evening she was on his sofa when the agency’s email came. She read the first page, and the second, and went back to the first.

“Pengcheng? Did you do this?”

He came in from the kitchen drying his hands and looked at the screen. “Yes. Last week.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I was going to.”

“When?” She turned the laptop back towards herself. “This is my contract. Why am I finding out from my agency?”

“Because I wanted the negotiation finished before I involved you. So you wouldn’t have to worry about it.”

She closed the laptop. “Was my original contract bad?”

He explained, calmly and exactly: the publicity obligations, the termination clause, the ambiguity in the overseas arrangements. She listened. She understood most of it. She was young, not stupid.

“And you negotiated all of it yourself. Without telling me.”

“Yes.”

“Pengcheng. I know you’re a lawyer. But I’m not one of your cases.”

She wasn’t angry the way he’d braced for. She was quieter than usual, which was worse. He reached across the table and she didn’t take his hand.

“I wasn’t trying to decide anything for you.”

“You already did.” She looked at him. “The changes are good. I’m grateful. But next time, tell me. And let me decide whether I want them.”

He was silent a long moment. “All right.”

“Promise?”

“Yes.”

Only then did she take his hand. “Thank you anyway,” she said, and kissed his cheek, and went to wash her face.

He sat at the table with the laptop shut in front of him. It had been the right decision; he was certain of that. He’d protected her from terms that might have hurt her and from a negotiation she had neither the time nor the experience for. But somewhere between what she’d said and the quiet way she’d kept her hand back, he began to understand that doing something for someone and giving them the choice weren’t the same thing. He understood the distinction perfectly in law. He’d never thought it would matter so much at home.

She came back in one of his shirts, sleeves over her hands, and climbed onto the sofa and tucked herself against his side without a word.

“Still upset?”

“No. I just want you to remember. I like being looked after. I don’t want you to decide everything for me.”

“I understand.”

She looked at him, checking, and put her head on his shoulder, and a minute later picked up her phone and did something to it with her thumb, smiling to herself.

“What are you doing?”

“Renaming you.”

He looked over her shoulder. Where it had said Mr. Yang (Boring) since January, it now said Pengcheng (Boyfriend, Apparently).

“And what am I in yours? Show me.”

He didn’t move. She held out her hand. He gave her his phone, and she found herself, and read it, and looked at him.

“Miss Yen (Page Seventeen)? Still?”

“It’s accurate.”

“You’re never going to change it, are you?”

“No,” said Pengcheng, and she laughed and kissed the corner of his mouth, and fell asleep against him ten minutes later with one hand flat over his heart, where she’d found out it was loud. He stayed where he was with his book open and unread on his knee, and didn’t move her, because moving her would have been unnecessarily cruel.

chapters.title: Her Sisters
chapters.desc: Dinner with her triplet sisters, who interrogate him. Si-Jie talks; Si-Wei watches. He says he’d never ask her to stop acting, even if his family disagrees. Two votes to one.
chapters.content:
Yang Pengcheng had cross-examined witnesses who were less frightening than the two women sitting across the table from him, and he was beginning to regret accepting dinner.

It wasn’t the restaurant, which was good, or the food, which was better. It was that Yen Si-Yuan had neglected to mention that meeting her sisters would take the form of a formal assessment of his suitability, and he was fairly sure neither of them intended to make it easy.

“You’re twenty-five?”

That was Yen Si-Jie, on his left: open face, quick eyes, hair tied loosely at the nape, and an extraordinary ability to ask three questions before anyone had finished answering the first. She’d been smiling at him since he arrived.

Beside her sat Yen Si-Wei, who’d said almost nothing, and was currently looking at him over the rim of her glass.

“Yes.”

“And you’re a lawyer. Corporate? At your family’s chambers? Is your father a lawyer too? And your mother?”

“Primarily. Yes. Yes. Senior counsel.”

“Oh, that’s interesting.” Si-Jie turned to her sister. “See? Interesting.”

Si-Wei didn’t respond. Beside him, Si-Yuan was trying hard not to laugh. He glanced at her, and she gave him an encouraging smile that encouraged nothing.

“Si-Jie, you’re asking too many questions.”

“I’m getting to know him.”

“You’ve been getting to know him for twenty minutes.”

“Exactly. I’m being efficient.”

Pengcheng put his chopsticks down. “It’s all right.”

“See? He’s nice,” said Si-Jie.

Si-Wei looked at him. “That’s what we’re trying to establish.”

Si-Yuan put her hand over her mouth. Pengcheng looked at Si-Wei for a second. “I understand,” he said, and Si-Wei nodded once and went back to her food, and somehow that was worse than all the questions put together.

✦ ✦ ✦

The dinner had been Si-Yuan’s idea. It was Saturday the twenty-first of May 2022, three months after a car park and a pair of borrowed slippers, and she’d wanted him to meet her sisters properly: not at the studio, not over a hurried phone call, not as the production lawyer who sometimes turned up with food. She’d told him Si-Jie was easy to talk to. She’d described Si-Wei as quiet but friendly. She’d said nothing whatsoever about an interrogation.

He leaned towards her. “Easy to talk to?”

She bit back a laugh. “Very. You’re doing well.”

“How reassuring.”

She squeezed his knee under the table, and Si-Jie’s eyes lit up at once.

“Does she do that often?”

He looked down at Si-Yuan’s hand. “Sometimes. More often when she wants something.”

“Pengcheng. You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I am.”

“You’re not acting like it.”

Si-Jie laughed. “Oh, I like him.”

“Don’t decide so quickly,” said Si-Wei, reaching for the dish of greens.

By the second course Si-Jie had established that he’d been to a good university, came from an old legal family, had no plans to leave the chambers, lived alone, could cook within a limited range, and had been seeing their sister for three months. That last fact got the most attention.

“Three months? Why didn’t you tell us?”

“Because I wanted to keep it,” said Si-Yuan.

“That’s not a reason.”

“It’s mine.”

“Did you tell Mum? Does she know?”

Si-Yuan hesitated. “Probably.”

“How?”

Si-Yuan looked at Pengcheng, and he looked back at her, and neither of them answered, and Si-Jie put her chopsticks down slowly.

“Wait. Does everyone know except us?”

“No,” said Si-Yuan quickly.

Si-Wei spoke for the first time in several minutes. “The make-up team knows.”

“How do you know that?”

“You posted a photograph of him bringing you coffee.”

“That doesn’t mean anything.”

“You put a heart beside his name.”

Si-Jie burst out laughing. Si-Yuan looked genuinely betrayed. “You went through my posts?”

“I saw it last week.”

“Why didn’t you say anything?”

Si-Wei looked at her. “You looked happy.”

The table went quiet. Si-Yuan blinked, and her face went soft, and Si-Jie looked from one sister to the other and smiled. “Well. I suppose that’s settled, then.”

Pengcheng had been listening. He looked at Si-Wei. “You’re observant.”

“I have to be,” she said, neither friendly nor unfriendly: a reminder that she was paying attention.

“I see,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Jie leaned in again. “Can I ask something? Do you like her?”

Si-Yuan nearly choked on her tea. “Si-Jie! You can’t just ask that!”

“He’s your boyfriend. That’s exactly why I can ask.” She turned to Pengcheng. “Well?”

He put his chopsticks down. Si-Yuan looked at him with her face already warm. She knew he wasn’t expressive. She knew he wasn’t the kind of man who’d launch into a declaration in front of her sisters. But she wanted to hear what he’d say, too.

“Yes.”

“How much?”

“Please,” said Si-Yuan into her hands.

He considered it. “Enough to come here tonight knowing I’d be questioned.”

Si-Jie laughed. “That’s a good answer.”

“It doesn’t tell us anything,” said Si-Wei.

“Then what would you like to know?”

She put her chopsticks down. “Why her?”

Si-Yuan went still. Si-Jie looked at her sister. “Si-Wei. That’s a bit harsh.”

“It’s a simple question.”

He didn’t seem to take offence. He thought about it, and then he answered it.

“She’s easy to be around. She talks when she wants to talk. She tells me when she’s unhappy. She laughs at things that aren’t funny.”

“Excuse me?” said Si-Yuan.

“And she works hard. She takes her work seriously even when she’s exhausted. She cares about people more than she lets anyone see.” He glanced at her. “She’s also very stubborn.”

“Pengcheng!”

“Which is occasionally difficult.” He looked back at Si-Wei. “And I like her. That’s why.”

Si-Wei held his eyes for a few seconds without saying anything. Then she picked up her glass. “All right.”

It fell some way short of an endorsement, and a long way short of a no. Si-Yuan let out a breath she hadn’t known she was holding.

✦ ✦ ✦

The questions went on. Whether he meant to marry. Si-Yuan nearly dropped her spoon. Whether he’d prefer a quiet wife or an ambitious one. He said he didn’t think those were mutually exclusive. Then Si-Wei asked whether he’d expect Si-Yuan to give up acting if they married, and this time he answered without any hesitation at all.

“No.”

“Even if your family disagrees?”

“That’s something I’d have to deal with.”

“Would you?”

He met her eyes. “Yes.”

Si-Yuan looked down at her plate. She didn’t know why the answer made her feel so warm. Perhaps because he’d said it so plainly. Perhaps because he hadn’t glanced towards his mother, or his father, or his surname, before he answered. He’d just said yes.

Si-Jie had found something else to investigate. “Have you introduced her to your parents?”

“Not formally.”

“Why not?”

“We haven’t been together very long.”

“Do they know about her?”

A brief silence. “Yes.”

Si-Yuan looked at him. He hadn’t told her that.

“What do they think?”

He reached for his tea. “My mother has opinions.”

“About Si-Yuan?”

“About the idea of my seeing an actress.”

The table changed. Si-Yuan’s fingers tightened on her chopsticks. Si-Jie stopped smiling, and even Si-Wei looked up.

“What did she say?” said Si-Yuan, low.

“It’s nothing you need to worry about.”

“Pengcheng.”

He knew that tone. It was the one she used when she wanted the truth, and he put his cup down. “She doesn’t think we’re a sensible match. Different backgrounds. Different professions. Different expectations.”

“That’s ridiculous. Has she met Si-Yuan?” said Si-Jie.

“Not yet.”

“Then how can she decide?”

He didn’t answer. Si-Wei was watching him. “And what do you think?”

“I think I know who I’m seeing,” said Pengcheng.

Si-Wei held his gaze a moment longer and looked down. This time she nearly smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

Pudding came late, and Si-Jie had ordered too much of it, and Si-Yuan accused her of doing it on purpose, and Si-Wei, without a word, took the last piece of cake while the other two were arguing about who’d eaten more at their birthday dinner in December. For a few minutes the interrogation was forgotten, and Pengcheng watched.

He was beginning to understand that Si-Yuan’s habit of talking with her hands hadn’t developed in isolation. Si-Jie’s was worse. Si-Wei said little, and when she did both of her sisters reacted at once. They interrupted each other and finished each other’s sentences and argued about things that didn’t matter, and every few minutes one of them stole something off another’s plate. He watched Si-Yuan laugh at something Si-Jie said, with her head tipped back and her eyes creased shut. She looked younger like this than the actress who knew her marks and her lines, or the girl who could sit through a contract negotiation without losing her temper: a sister, between two people who’d known her since before she could remember anything.

He found he was smiling. Si-Wei noticed, and didn’t say so. She only moved the dish of cut fruit a few centimetres towards him across the tablecloth, which, he would learn much later, was the most Si-Wei ever said to anyone she’d decided to keep.

He paid before Si-Yuan could reach for her bag. Si-Jie looked impressed. Si-Wei looked at the receipt.

“You’re paying? Why?”

“Because I invited you.”

“Good answer,” said Si-Jie.

At the door the two of them stopped. “We’ll get a car,” Si-Jie announced.

“I live in the same direction,” said Si-Yuan.

“Exactly,” said Si-Jie sweetly, and took Si-Wei by the arm and walked off. Si-Wei looked back once, from her sister to Pengcheng, gave her a small nod, and kept walking.

“They’re terrible,” said Si-Yuan, when they’d gone round the corner.

“They care about you.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No,” he agreed.

“Did you like them?”

“Yes. Si-Jie talks a lot. Si-Wei doesn’t.”

“She’s just quiet.”

“I noticed.”

She looked up at him. “Did you pass?”

He glanced back at the restaurant. “That remains to be seen.”

They’d almost reached the car park when her phone buzzed.

Si-Jie (Questions): We’re still here. Look behind you.

She turned. Across the street, behind the restaurant’s glass, two figures were standing by the window. Si-Jie was practically pressed against it, waving. Si-Wei stood beside her holding her phone.

“Oh my God.”

Her phone buzzed again.

Si-Wei (Watching): Don’t let him drive tired.

“Should I wave?” said Pengcheng.

“No! Ignore them.” She turned her back on the window firmly. “Si-Jie likes you. Si-Wei hasn’t decided.”

“And you?”

“I’m still considering.”

He stepped closer. “That’s unfortunate. I’ve already decided.”

Her face changed. “About what?”

He brushed a piece of hair off her cheek. “That I like you.”

She looked at him, and at his mouth, and he saw her look and waited, the way he always waited, and she put both hands flat on his chest and kissed him in the car park, properly, not the quick surprised kiss in his car three months before but a long one, with his arm coming round her waist and her mouth smiling against his.

When she drew back she stayed close. “Do you think they saw?”

He looked over her head. Si-Jie was jumping up and down. Si-Wei had lowered her phone.

“I think so.”

“Wonderful.” She caught his sleeve before he could open the car door. “Pengcheng. Thank you for coming. For meeting them.”

“I wanted to.”

“I love that you wanted to,” she said, and kissed him once more, and this time he held her there a while, with one hand at her waist, and didn’t say anything, and didn’t need to.

Behind the window Si-Jie grabbed her sister’s arm. “Look. They’re kissing again.”

“I have eyes.”

“He’s actually very handsome.”

“You said that ten minutes ago.” Si-Wei watched the car park for a second longer. “Two votes to one.”

“What?”

“He’s passed. For now,” said Si-Wei, and Si-Jie squeaked and got her phone out.

Si-Jie (Questions): CONGRATULATIONS YOU HAVE BEEN APPROVED

Si-Wei (Watching): Don’t make her cry.

Si-Yuan read the second one twice, and her smile went into something quieter. She put her arms round his waist at the open car door and pressed her cheek against his chest.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. My sisters like you. Si-Wei says you’re not to make me cry.”

His hand on the back of her head stopped moving for a second. “I’ll try not to.”

“Promise?”

“I’ll do my best.”

It wasn’t quite a promise, and she noticed. But she believed him, and for now that was enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her home, and then drove himself home, and at the second red light his phone lit up on the passenger seat with a number he didn’t know.

Unknown number: This is Si-Jie. Si-Wei says I’m not allowed to text you. Drive carefully. You passed. Mostly.

He looked at it until the light changed. At home, before he took his jacket off, he saved the number. He typed Yen Si-Jie, and then, after a moment’s thought, added (Sister, Talkative). Then his phone went again.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): I miss you already.

Pengcheng: You saw me twenty minutes ago.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): That’s a long time.

He looked at the screen. He typed four words and looked at them, and deleted them, and typed them again, and sent them before he could think better of it, because nobody had asked him to.

Pengcheng: I miss you too.

The answer came at once, three hearts and nothing else, and he put the phone face up on the table and stood in his quiet kitchen with his jacket still on. At twenty-five he’d been introduced to two sisters, subjected to a character assessment over dinner, and informed that his suitability remained under review. He’d survived, just. And judging by the phone lighting up again on the table, he’d acquired two more people who’d be keeping an eye on him from now on. He didn’t know what he’d done to deserve that. He found that he didn’t mind at all.

chapters.title: The First Bow
chapters.desc: Lunar New Year at his mother’s house. Her grandfather-in-law’s portrait; a bow lower than she’s ever bowed. His mother speaks only to him all afternoon. In the car he holds her hand and says nothing.
chapters.epigraph: “I just wanted her to like me.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Yen Si-Yuan noticed about the house was the portrait.

It hung in the middle of the main wall of the reception room in a dark wooden frame, high enough that anyone coming in had to look up at it: an old man in a judge’s robes in a carved chair, hands on its arms, eyes straight ahead and unsmiling, the background so dark that only the white of his collar and the silver at his temples came out of it.

She stopped for half a second. Pengcheng, beside her, noticed.

“My grandfather,” he said, low.

“Was he a judge?”

“Chief justice.”

“Oh,” said Si-Yuan, and looked at the portrait again.

It was Sunday the twenty-second of January 2023, the first day of the Lunar New Year, eleven months after a car park and a pair of borrowed slippers, and the first time he’d brought her home. The house had the weight of important people who’d lived in it for generations. The shelves held leather spines. The cabinets held photographs of men in robes, framed certificates, family papers. Even the flowers on the table looked chosen for their restraint. And she was standing in the middle of it in a pale cream dress with a gift box held in both hands, trying not to look as nervous as she was.

“Is your mother here? Does she know I’m coming?”

“I told her.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

His face softened a fraction. “She knows.”

“Okay.”

He reached for the box. “I’ll take that. Your hands are cold.”

“They’re not.”

He touched her fingers. They were. He took the box anyway and left her with her bag, and at the doorway she straightened the cuff of her dress.

“You’re nervous.”

“No.” He waited. “A little.”

“Stay beside me,” he said, and the plainness of it made her feel better. She slipped her hand into his, and they went in together.

✦ ✦ ✦

His mother was standing by the tea table in dark red silk, the colour of good fortune, with small jade earrings and her hair pinned neatly, talking to an older relative. Her eyes came to her son.

“You’re late.”

“Happy New Year, Mother.”

Si-Yuan let go of his hand and stepped forward and bowed. It was a proper bow, not hurried and not careless; she bent lower than she ever had to anyone, with her back straight and her hands together in front of her. When she came up she held the box out with both hands.

“Happy New Year, Madam Yang. I’ve brought something for you. I hope you’ll accept it.”

His mother looked at the box, and at her.

“You’re the actress.”

It wasn’t a question. Si-Yuan’s smile stayed where it was. “Yes, Madam.”

Madam Yang didn’t take the gift. She looked at her son. “You said you were bringing a guest.”

“She is my guest.”

Only then did his mother take the box. “Thank you.”

Si-Yuan bowed her head again. “You’re welcome.”

“Your uncle’s in the study. He’s been asking about the new case. And your grandfather’s old colleagues are here. Your grandfather would have been pleased to see the family gathered today.” She turned away. “Come. The others are waiting.”

And that was the end of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunch was in the long dining room, and there were more people than Si-Yuan had expected: uncles, aunts, cousins, family friends, several old men whose names were gone from her head as soon as she’d been told them. Everyone knew everyone. The talk moved easily from appointments to property, from schools overseas to the latest judgments in the courts. There was a particular confidence in the room, the confidence of people who’d grown up knowing their surname would open doors.

She sat beside Pengcheng. His mother sat at the head of the table.

“Your father tells me you’ve taken on the arbitration,” said an elderly uncle across the table.

“Yes.”

“Complicated?”

“No.”

The old man laughed. “Your grandfather would have liked that answer.”

His mother served him a piece of fish. “Your grandfather always said a lawyer should know the difference between a complicated matter and a man making it look complicated. Have you spoken to the senior partner?”

“Yesterday.”

“And?”

“We’re waiting for the documents.”

His mother nodded, and asked about another case, and another, and then a meeting with one of the family’s oldest clients. She didn’t look at Si-Yuan once: not when the dishes went round, or when someone asked whether Pengcheng would come to the gathering that evening, or when the aunt beside her admired Si-Yuan’s dress. She talked to her son like he was the only person sitting next to her.

Si-Yuan had braced herself for difficult questions, and found that there being no questions at all was somehow worse. She’d expected to be asked about acting, about her family, her education, what she meant to do with her life. She’d rehearsed answers in the car. She’d thought about how to explain that acting wasn’t something she did lightly, that she understood what a public career asked of a person. She’d even prepared herself to smile through a remark about how unstable the industry was. There was nothing. No curiosity. No attempt to know her. She might have been a piece of furniture he’d carried in with him: present, visible, not worth addressing.

“Pengcheng, did you send the documents to Mr. Liang?”

“This morning.”

“Your father thinks you should take more responsibility for the family’s commercial clients.”

“I already handle several.”

“Not enough. Your grandfather never waited to be told he was ready.”

Pengcheng’s hand paused on his chopsticks. “Grandfather had his own way of doing things.”

“And you have yours,” said his mother: an expectation dressed up as conversation, sitting somewhere between praise and a warning.

Si-Yuan looked at her plate. She’d been eating slowly, careful not to reach across anyone or interrupt anyone older. She’d smiled when she was spoken to, and thanked the aunt who’d passed her a dish. She was trying hard. An uncle asked her whether she was enjoying the food.

“Very much. Thank you.”

“Do you usually eat this sort of thing?”

“Not often. My family has a simpler New Year lunch.”

“Ah. Well. It’s good to experience different things,” said the uncle, and turned back to the man beside him.

She felt Pengcheng’s knee touch hers under the table: a question. She turned her head and he was looking at her. She smiled at him to say I’m fine, and he looked at her a second longer.

“Pengcheng. Did you hear what I said?”

He turned back to his mother. “Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Halfway through the meal an old man mentioned the portrait. “It’s been restored, hasn’t it? It looks very well.”

“Before the New Year. He deserved to be remembered properly.” His mother glanced at her son. “Pengcheng. Do you remember what your grandfather used to say about the family?”

“Which thing?”

“That a family name is not something you borrow. You carry it. And that the people who carry it must understand what is expected of them.”

The table went quiet for a breath. Si-Yuan felt it before she understood it. The words hadn’t been aimed at her. They hadn’t needed to be.

“I remember,” said Pengcheng.

“Good,” said his mother, and lifted her tea, and the talk moved on.

Si-Yuan looked up at the portrait. The old judge looked down on all of them. She wondered whether he’d have thought her unsuitable too, and whether the people in this house had decided that before she’d come through the door. Her throat went tight. She swallowed and went on eating.

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch, when the guests went back to the reception room, she helped an aunt carry a tray of teacups to the kitchen.

“Oh, no, no, you’re a guest.”

“It’s all right. I’d like to help.”

“You’re very polite,” said the aunt, smiling, and Si-Yuan smiled back and carried the tray in.

The housekeeper took it from her. “Miss Yen, leave that with me.” She hesitated, and then said, low, “Please don’t worry. Madam is like this with everyone.”

Si-Yuan looked at her. The housekeeper seemed to realise she’d said too much, and dropped her eyes. “Please enjoy the rest of your visit.”

When she came back into the reception room he was by the windows with an uncle and his mother, and he saw her at once. His eyes went over her face, and he excused himself and came across.

“Have you eaten enough? Are you tired? We can go soon.”

She looked towards his mother. “Shouldn’t we stay longer? It’s New Year. We shouldn’t leave early.”

He looked at her face, and nodded. “All right.”

He didn’t argue, or tell her he wanted to leave. He stayed. She was grateful for it.

They left a little after three. She bowed to the old relatives first and to his mother last.

“Thank you for having me, Madam Yang. Happy New Year.”

“Happy New Year.”

Si-Yuan waited. Perhaps there’d be something else: a polite word, something about the food, one sentence that would make the afternoon feel less like an exam she’d never been allowed to sit.

His mother turned to her son. “Don’t forget to ring your father tomorrow. And speak to Mr. Liang before Monday. Drive carefully.”

“Goodbye, Mother.”

Si-Yuan bowed once more and followed him outside, and the door closed behind them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car was quiet. He started the engine and didn’t move off. She sat with her hands folded in her lap, and they’d gone cold again.

“Are you all right?”

“Yes.”

He didn’t drive. “Si-Yuan. Look at me.”

She did. Her smile was still there, but smaller, the one she used when she didn’t want anyone to worry. He reached across the console and took her hand, and her fingers went into his, and he rubbed his thumb over her knuckles. Through the windscreen she could still see the doorway where she’d bowed twice.

“Was I polite enough?”

His thumb stopped. “What?”

“To your mother. Did I bow properly? Was it too much? Did I say anything wrong?”

“You were polite. Yes. No. No.”

She looked out of the window. “Okay. I just wanted her to like me.”

It was so quiet he nearly wished she hadn’t said it.

He wanted to tell her that his mother was difficult with everyone, that she’d spent her whole life measuring people against a standard nobody could meet, that he’d learned long ago not to take any of it personally. He wanted to tell her none of it mattered. He knew none of that was quite true. It mattered to her. She’d come because he’d asked her. She’d chosen a dress and bought a present and rehearsed her greeting and bowed lower than she’d ever bowed to anybody, and his mother had talked to him for the whole of the afternoon. He’d seen it happen. He’d been sitting right there. He’d let it.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“For what?” She tried to smile. “It’s all right. It’s the first time. Maybe she needs time.”

He didn’t say anything.

“She’s important to you,” said Si-Yuan.

“That doesn’t mean you have to be uncomfortable.”

“I wasn’t uncomfortable.” He looked at her. She sighed. “All right. A little.” She watched his thumb move on her hand. “Your grandfather’s portrait was beautiful. He looked very serious. Did you know him well?”

“Not as well as I’d have liked. He was strict. He didn’t say much.”

“Like you.”

“Perhaps.”

“Did he love your grandmother?”

He looked at her. “That’s a strange question. I don’t know.”

“That’s sad,” said Si-Yuan, and rested her head back against the seat, and laid her hand over his on the console. He turned his palm up and let her hold it, and they sat a minute longer in the car outside the house, and then he put it into gear.

✦ ✦ ✦

At his flat she changed into a loose jumper and sat on the sofa while he made tea. He’d offered to order dinner and she’d said she wasn’t hungry, and he’d made tea anyway. When he came back she was looking at her phone.

“Your sisters?”

“Si-Jie. She asked how it went. I said fine.”

He put the cup down. “Was it?”

She looked at him, and smiled. “Mostly.”

He sat beside her and she leaned into his shoulder, and they watched the television without seeing any of it.

“Do you think your mother dislikes me?”

“I don’t know. I don’t think she knows you well enough to dislike you.”

She considered that. “Maybe.” Her fingers traced the lines of his palm. “She never asked me anything. Not about my work, or my family. She only talked to you.”

He looked down at their hands. “Yes.”

“Maybe next time,” said Si-Yuan.

“Maybe,” he said.

She kissed his cheek. “Happy New Year.”

“Happy New Year.”

She kissed him again, nearer the corner of his mouth, and he caught her hand before she could take it away, and turned his head and kissed her properly, slow and familiar and warm. When he drew back she stayed close.

“You’re quiet. What are you thinking about?”

He looked at her before he answered. “That you shouldn’t have had to work so hard today.”

Her face went soft, and she touched his cheek. “I wanted to. Because it’s your family. And because I love you.”

The words came easily to her now. He’d heard them in messages and in whispers in the dark, and every time she said them to his face, something in his changed. He didn’t say them back. He held her against him on the sofa, with his hand over hers, and outside the city was still celebrating; somewhere nearby fireworks cracked against the evening sky, and the windows shook a little in their frames.

She closed her eyes. For the rest of the evening he said almost nothing, and she didn’t ask him to. She thought his silence meant he understood. She thought his hand over hers was his way of telling her she’d done well, and that she belonged next to him, and that nothing his mother thought could change what he felt. She fell asleep against him on the sofa believing all of it, and he sat still so as not to wake her, with the fireworks going on and on over the harbour, and the gift box she’d chosen still unopened on a table in his mother’s house.

chapters.title: Morality Clause
chapters.desc: A photograph under the studio’s side entrance, and the studio reaches for clause fourteen. He answers in thirteen pages, as her lawyer, without raising his voice, and wins. She can’t thank him in public, so she thanks him in his office at midnight: explicit, on his desk.
chapters.epigraph: “You never have to apologise for loving someone.”
chapters.content:
The photograph was taken just before midnight on a Thursday in March 2023, under the side entrance of the studio, in the rain.

They’d stood there for less than two minutes. He’d come from a meeting with dinner in a bag, because he knew that otherwise she’d say she wasn’t hungry. He’d taken her bag. She’d reached up and straightened his tie. He’d said something she couldn’t hear over the rain, and she’d laughed, and he’d bent his head and kissed her cheek. That was all.

By breakfast it was on the front of an entertainment paper.

RISING ACTRESS YEN SI-YUAN’S MYSTERY BOYFRIEND REVEALED?

It was grainy and taken from across the street. His face was clear in profile. Hers was mostly hidden by her hair, but there was no mistaking the coat, or the costume, or how close she was standing. The caption was worse: Sources suggest the actress may be involved with a senior legal representative connected to her production company.

She read it twice on the edge of her bed in her pyjamas, with her breakfast going cold, and rang him.

“Have you seen it?”

“Yes.”

“Who is he? My mystery boyfriend.”

She could hear him not smiling. “He’s very handsome.”

“He’s also very annoying.”

“That’s unfortunate.” Then, more evenly: “I’m more concerned that they’ve made a photograph of me holding your handbag look like an investigative breakthrough.”

She laughed, and stopped. “They’ll ring the studio. And my agency.”

“They already have, probably.”

He heard her breathing change. “Si-Yuan. Don’t read the comments.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You’re lying. Eat your breakfast.”

“You’re very bossy.”

“And you’re very predictable,” he said, and she laughed again, and it sounded more like her.

“Don’t worry about the photograph.”

“I won’t,” she said. He didn’t believe her. Neither did she.

✦ ✦ ✦

The studio rang him at a quarter past ten. By eleven he was in a conference room with three of the production company’s lawyers and a printed copy of the paper in the middle of the table, beside her original talent agreement.

The legal director, a heavy-lidded man called Mr. Tam, tapped the document. “Clause fourteen.”

Pengcheng knew it by heart. It was broad enough to make a junior lawyer uncomfortable and vague enough to make a senior one dangerous: the company could act if an artist’s conduct was considered likely to damage its reputation, the production, or its commercial relationships. It had survived for years because nobody had thought to challenge it.

“The photograph has attracted attention,” said Mr. Tam.

“Attention isn’t damage.”

“It concerns a private relationship with someone connected to the production.”

“With production counsel.”

“That’s precisely the problem. We’d prefer you to step away from the matter.”

“She’s my client.”

“She’s an actress under contract with this company. Pengcheng, don’t make this personal.”

“It became personal when you sent her agency a letter asking for an explanation under clause fourteen because a newspaper photographed her standing next to me.” He didn’t raise his voice. “Has an advertiser complained?”

“Not yet.”

“Has a broadcaster objected? Has filming been disrupted? Has she missed a promotional obligation?”

“No.”

He closed the agreement. “Then what exactly are we investigating? You have a photograph of two adults outside a studio. There’s no misconduct, no breach of confidentiality, no disruption, and no term anywhere requiring her to disclose who she sees.”

“Clause fourteen—”

“Is not a licence to regulate her private life.”

His voice never went up, and the room went quiet.

“We’ll need a formal response,” said Mr. Tam at last. “And you’ll disclose the relationship?”

“I’ve disclosed it already, to the people it needed disclosing to. Anything where my involvement could compromise independent advice will go to other counsel, with her agreement.” He stood. “But I’m not withdrawing from this response. I’m her lawyer until she tells me otherwise. You might remember that before you send another letter.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Yuan was in a costume fitting when her manager gave her the notice. Potential reputational exposure. Commercial considerations. Request for clarification regarding the nature of the relationship. It made her feel she’d done something shameful: as though standing next to someone she loved was an offence that needed explaining.

Her manager pulled up a chair. “Don’t panic. Pengcheng rang this morning. He’s at the studio now. He’s writing the response.”

She folded the letter carefully, and couldn’t say anything, and then said, “Okay.” She wasn’t. But she knew he was there, and that was enough to keep her from crying in the middle of a fitting with a seamstress pinning her hem.

At lunch Fong found her on an apple box behind the soundstage, not eating, with the folded letter on her knee. The assistant director sat down beside her without asking, headset round her neck, and unwrapped a sandwich and held out half.

Fong chewed. “I’ve seen that clause used twice in eleven years. Both times on men who’d actually done something. Never on a girl for standing next to her boyfriend in the rain. I told you once he was thorough. You remember? Thorough’s rare round here.”

“You said I’d be glad of it one day.”

“Today’s the day,” said Fong, and got up, and went off across the lot shouting into her headset about a generator, and Si-Yuan sat with half a sandwich in her hand and found she could eat it.

✦ ✦ ✦

His response was thirteen pages. It dealt with the wording of clause fourteen, the absence of any demonstrable harm, the company’s obligation to act reasonably, and the limits of its authority over an artist’s private conduct. He attached the revised agreement he’d negotiated a year before, which the company had signed without much thought at the time. Now it mattered: the termination clause required written notice and a fair chance to respond, and no alleged breach could rest on speculation.

He hadn’t written it as an angry boyfriend. He’d written it as a lawyer who knew exactly what the other side was trying to do.

Just before six Mr. Tam put the pages down. “We’ll withdraw the notice.”

“Confirm it in writing.”

“You’re very thorough.”

“It’s my job.”

There was no slammed door, no raised voice, no announcement. Only a written withdrawal and a legal director who’d become interested in his next appointment. Outside the building his phone was already going.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Did you win?

Pengcheng: The notice will be withdrawn.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): So yes?

Pengcheng: So yes.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): I knew you would. I’ve been telling the seamstress about you for an hour. She says you sound frightening.

He looked at that for longer than he needed to, and then rang her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He couldn’t go to the cast dinner that night. The photograph was still everywhere, there were reporters at the main entrance, and her agency had told her to say nothing at all. She couldn’t thank him in public. She couldn’t even say he’d represented her.
