The studio’s statement said only that the company had reviewed the matter and that no breach of contractual obligations had been established. Nothing about him. Nothing about thirteen pages, or a day spent defending her right to a private life in a room she wasn’t allowed into.

At a quarter past nine she sent a photograph: the dinner table, a half-eaten plate, a glass of water, and in one corner her fingers making a small heart.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): I can’t say anything here.

Pengcheng: You don’t need to.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): I want to see you.

His office was dark except for the desk lamp and the city coming in at the windows. He typed Come by when you’ve finished, and she answered at once, Really?, and he said yes. Then he opened the bottom drawer of his desk and moved a stack of files into it, off the desk, and didn’t let himself think too carefully about why.

She knocked a little before midnight. She’d changed out of the dinner dress into a soft pale cardigan over a plain top, with her hair loose and a paper bag in her hand.

“Dessert. Two pastries from the place by the studio. I was passing.”

“At eleven at night.”

“Yes,” she said innocently, and put the bag on the desk, and stepped into his arms.

He caught her round the waist. She pressed her face into his chest and held on.

“Thank you,” she said into his shirt.

“You don’t have to thank me.”

“I know. I’m going to anyway.” She pulled back and looked at him. “You won.”

“We resolved the matter.”

“That’s lawyer for winning. Let me be impressed with you, Pengcheng. All day I couldn’t say a word to anybody. Let me say it to you.”

Something in his face gave. “All right.”

She looked round the office: the neat desk, the full shelves, the files in exact stacks, a photograph of his grandfather by the window and a smaller one of his parents. “When I read that letter I wanted to ring you and ask you to make it disappear.”

“That isn’t how it works.”

“I know. But I knew you’d know what to do.” She leaned back against the edge of the desk. “Today I was frightened. I thought about all the work I’ve done, and everything I’m not allowed to do because I have to be careful, and I thought, what if they take it away because of one photograph?”

“You weren’t wrong to be frightened.” He came closer. “They have obligations, and so do you. They can’t threaten your career because they don’t like how something looks. And you don’t have to be grateful for being treated fairly.”

She looked at him a long moment. Then she took hold of his tie.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Is this why you cleared the desk?” she said against his mouth.

“I’m not answering that.”

“That’s a yes.”

She drew him in by the tie and kissed him, and the restraint he’d worn all day in a room full of lawyers went somewhere and didn’t come back. He kissed her hard and then slowly and then hard again, and she pushed his jacket off his shoulders and let it fall over the back of his chair. She sat up on the edge of the desk and pulled him between her knees.

“I couldn’t do anything for you today. Let me,” she said.

He undid her cardigan, and the top underneath, and stopped to look at her in the lamplight, the way he always looked, like he meant to remember. Then he put his mouth on her throat and worked down, without a word, as he always did, slow and exact, until she had both hands in his hair and her head back and was saying his name to the ceiling of his office. She pulled at his belt. He let her. He drew her skirt up her thighs and slid her underwear down and off, and she wrapped her legs round him and pulled him in against her, and he pushed into her slowly, all the way, on the edge of his own desk, and they both went still.

“Look at me,” she said.

He looked. He moved, slow and deep, one hand flat on the wood beside her hip and the other spread across her lower back holding her to him, and she held his face and watched him the way he’d watched her in every meeting she’d never been allowed into. His breathing went ragged. The lamp shook a little on its stand. She felt it building in her, and in him, and she said into his ear, don’t stop, don’t you dare stop, and he didn’t, and she came with her heels in the small of his back and her mouth against his neck to keep the sound in. He followed a moment after, holding her so tight she couldn’t breathe, his face in her hair, with the one low broken sound she’d only ever heard from him like this.

Afterwards they ended up on the sofa by the window, her cardigan on the floor and his tie somewhere under the desk, her head on his chest.

“Did you know I couldn’t thank you in public?”

“I assumed.”

“Did you mind? You did all that, and nobody knows.”

“I didn’t do it to be known.”

“I know. Still, I wanted to.”

“Then you have.”

“Not enough,” said Si-Yuan, and he looked down at her.

“You’re trouble.”

“Your trouble,” she said, and he didn’t correct her.

She kissed him once and put her forehead against his. “Thank you for being my lawyer today. And my boyfriend. And for not letting them make me feel I’d done something wrong.”

He went still. “You never have to apologise for loving someone.”

She looked at him like she might say something else. She didn’t. and tucked herself back into his chest. On the desk, under the folder, the withdrawal lay on top of thirteen pages: no breach established. Matter resolved. The pastries were still in their bag. Neither of them had eaten one, and at one in the morning she remembered and sat up and made him have half of hers, on the sofa, in the dark, and told him with her mouth full that he’d been frightening in a room she’d never seen, and that the seamstress had been right.

In the morning the withdrawal came through in writing at five past nine, as he’d asked, and he forwarded it to her without a word of his own. She read it on set between takes, in costume, and saved it in a folder on her phone that she named Clause Fourteen. She never told him the folder existed. It was the first thing she’d ever kept of his that he hadn’t meant her to keep.

chapters.title: Her Award
chapters.desc: Best New Actress. He’s three rows behind as her lawyer and can’t stand when she does. A kiss behind a backstage curtain. White lilies at her hotel from his mother, with no card. He promises the front row.
chapters.content:
Yang Pengcheng had been told to sit three rows behind the nominees, which was reasonable. He was there as Yen Si-Yuan’s legal representative, not her boyfriend. The production company had invited several people from legal and management, and he was needed: the ceremony came with contractual appearances, press arrangements and two sponsorship obligations whose wording he’d already corrected twice. He’d done everything required of him. And now he was in the third row in the spring of 2023, watching the woman he loved wait to hear her name.

He applauded when appropriate. He stood when the room stood. He listened to the presenters with the polite attention he gave people speaking in meetings. His eyes kept going back to the front.

She was in a soft champagne dress, plain in its line, her hair swept up off her neck and small earrings catching the stage lights whenever she turned her head. He’d told her at the hotel that she looked beautiful, and she’d asked whether he was sure, because the stylist had changed the earrings at the last minute. He’d said he was sure. She’d spent five more minutes on her bracelet.

Under the lights she looked almost impossibly composed. Almost. He knew the signs: her fingers moving against the programme in her lap, her shoulders a fraction too still, her lips pressing together each time a presenter paused before a name. She’d been nervous for three days. She’d said she didn’t expect to win and then asked him whether her performance had been good enough. She’d said she didn’t care about awards and then spent twenty minutes deciding on a dress. He’d heard every version of the question, and given the same answer every time. You did well. He hadn’t said it to stop her worrying. He’d said it because it was true.

“And now, for Best New Actress.”

He sat a little straighter. Her name came up on the screen behind the presenter with the others, and he watched her smile politely while her eyes went perfectly still.

“And the award goes to Yen Si-Yuan, for The Season We Left Behind.”

For half a second she didn’t move. Then her hand went to her mouth, and the actress beside her turned and hugged her, and she laughed, startled, and stood.

He stood with the room and clapped. Once, twice. Then he forgot to count.

She walked to the stage with one hand flat on her chest and a smile on her face that didn’t quite believe itself, and at the steps she glanced down to make sure she wouldn’t catch her heel in the hem. He knew that habit. He knew how she looked when she was trying not to cry. He knew she’d forget half the speech she’d written, and he knew that when she looked out at the audience she’d look for him.

She did. Three rows back. Her smile changed when she found him: smaller and warmer, and entirely hers. Something pulled tight in his chest. He wanted to be nearer. He wanted to walk to the steps and take her hand, to be the first face she saw when she came down, not a man behind a row of strangers who knew him as her lawyer. He stayed where he was, and kept applauding.

“Thank you.” Her voice shook a little at the microphone. “I prepared a speech because everyone told me to, and I think I’ve forgotten most of it.”

The room laughed. She thanked the director and the crew and everyone who’d trusted her with the part, and said there’d been days she was more difficult than she’d realised, and the room laughed again. Then her hands tightened on the award.

“And to my family. Thank you for believing in me when I wasn’t sure I could do this.”

She didn’t mention him. She couldn’t. The photograph was barely a month old and the studio had only just withdrawn its notice under clause fourteen. He understood. He’d never expected her to. Still, when she looked down at the award and smiled to herself, he felt a small, unreasonable ache. He wanted to be part of her happiness out loud, not folded into a professional obligation in the third row. Beside her.

As she turned to go she looked out once more. He gave her a small nod, a private congratulations, and she smiled, and that carried her off the stage.

✦ ✦ ✦

Backstage was crowded with publicists, assistants, photographers, stylists, somebody calling for the next presenter. She was surrounded at once. Her manager was nearly in tears.

“You’re an award-winning actress.”

“Don’t say it like that. Say it like I’m still me.”

“Unfortunately you’re still you,” said her manager, and they both laughed, and somebody gave her a bouquet from the production company and somebody else wanted five minutes for an interview. She answered everyone. She was so happy she could barely keep her face straight. And every few seconds she looked towards the corridor.

Her manager noticed. “He’s by the press room. Talking to the organisers.”

Si-Yuan handed her the award. “Hold this.”

“Si-Yuan—”

She was already gone. He’d just finished explaining to a man from the production company why the studio’s draft statement mustn’t imply that the award endorsed any commercial partner, and the man had said he’d revise it, and Pengcheng had looked past his shoulder and seen her at the end of the corridor. She wasn’t coming closer. She was waiting. He excused himself.

“Congratulations,” he said when he reached her.

“That’s all?”

“Would you prefer a formal statement? On behalf of your legal representative, congratulations on your first award.”

She stared at him and laughed. “You’re so annoying.” She looked down the corridor at the photographers near the entrance, and stepped closer. “Can I have a hug?”

He glanced round, and opened his arms, and she was in them before he’d finished.

He spoke into her hair. “Well done. You earned it.”

“I know. I mean, I think I did.”

“You did. Every second of it.”

“Did you see? All of it? Even when I nearly tripped?”

“It was a very small step.”

“It was not.”

“A little,” he admitted, and she laughed, and then her face went soft.

“I wanted to see you. And I couldn’t. Three rows behind. Do you know how far that is?”

“Approximately three rows.”

Her eyes had started to shine. He touched her cheek. “Don’t cry. Your make-up’s perfect.”

“That’s what you’re worried about?”

“No. I thought it might help.” He watched her. “What?”

She looked towards the side corridor. “Come with me. Somewhere without cameras.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The curtain was heavy dark velvet beside the narrow entrance to one of the small rooms backstage. It wasn’t private. There were people on the other side of the partition and the ceremony still coming through the walls. But for a minute the space behind it was empty, and she slipped behind it and he followed.

“Why did you bring me here?”

“Because I wanted to kiss you.”

“Someone could come through.”

“Then we’ll be quick,” she said, entirely unrepentant, and he shook his head and reached for her waist.

She put one hand on his shoulder and the other round the back of his neck and kissed him, and he held her carefully because of the dress and the earrings and the people a few steps away, and she kissed him again when he drew back, and again. At last he put his forehead against hers.

“Congratulations.”

“You’ve said that.”

“I didn’t say it properly.” His thumb moved along her waist. “I watched you up there and I thought, she did that herself. Nobody gave it to her. Not the studio, not me. She sat on apple boxes at four in the morning and did it. And I couldn’t stand up and say so.”

Her face changed. The smile stayed, and something behind it went soft. She kissed him again, slowly this time.

“You’re the first person I wanted to find.”

“I know. You looked at me before you’d finished the speech.”

“You noticed?”

“I notice you,” said Pengcheng.

Someone called her name on the other side of the curtain. She shut her eyes. He smiled.

“Go.”

She straightened his tie and smoothed his jacket, as if she hadn’t just kissed him behind a curtain. He caught her hand and kissed her knuckles. “Go and enjoy it.” She slipped out, and he waited until he heard her laugh in the corridor, and then straightened his jacket and followed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flowers came to her hotel room just before half past ten.

She was cross-legged on the sofa, still in the dress, with her hair half down and the award on the coffee table, reading her phone. Si-Jie had sent about twenty messages, three of them voice notes that were mostly screaming. She played the last one twice. Under the screaming, at the very end, her sister’s voice went normal: I watched Mum watch you. She held Baba’s hand the whole speech and she didn’t let go when they cut to the adverts. I’ve never seen her hold his hand in my life. Ring her tomorrow. Not tonight. Tonight’s yours. Si-Yuan sat with the phone against her ear for a while after it finished.

Si-Wei (Watching): You looked happy.

Si-Yuan: I was.

Si-Wei (Watching): Good. You deserved it.

She was still smiling when the hotel staff knocked with a large arrangement of white lilies: tall stems and dark leaves in a clear glass vase, elegant, expensive-looking, nothing extra.

“Who sent them?”

“There’s no message, Miss. Only your name.”

The card holder was empty. She looked at the delivery slip. The sender was a private residence, and she knew the address. Her smile went out of her face slowly.

White lilies. No card. She tried to find a kind reading. A traditional gesture, maybe. His mother acknowledging the award without wanting to write anything. Something sent because it was expected. She couldn’t quite settle on any of them.

Pengcheng (Boyfriend, Apparently): Are you back at the hotel? Did you eat?

Si-Yuan: Yes. Someone sent flowers. I think your mother.

There was no reply for a full minute. Then her phone rang.

“Was there a card?”

“No. Just the slip.”

“What are they?”

“White lilies.” She waited. “Do you think she sent them because of the award?”

“I don’t know.”

“They’re pretty,” she said. He was quiet, and she could hear traffic at his end.

“Do you want to come over?”

“Twenty minutes.”

He came in still in his suit, with his tie in his pocket and a paper bag from the noodle place near the venue in one hand, because he knew there’d been canapés and nothing else, and he was looking at the lilies before he’d looked at her. He picked up the slip, read it, and put it down.

“Do you think it’s a good sign?”

“I don’t know.”

“That’s all right.” She stood beside him. “I think I was hoping there’d be a card. Even just congratulations.”

She wasn’t asking him for anything. She wasn’t asking him to ring his mother. She was admitting that she’d wanted something small: a sentence, a name, a sign that the woman who’d talked past her all through New Year had noticed she’d done something that mattered.

He looked at the lilies a while. “She knows about the award. She might not know what to write.”

“Maybe.”

“Keep them, if you like them.”

“They’re beautiful,” said Si-Yuan, and put her arms round him, and he held her, and she said into his shirt that she liked hearing him tell her she’d done well, and he said he’d say it as often as she liked, and did.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate his noodles out of the cartons. She sat with the award in her lap and made him look at every photograph from the ceremony, although he’d been in the room for all of them. He looked at each one properly. At the last, a close-up with her eyes bright and her smile so wide her eyes had creased shut, he stopped.

“Keep this one.”

“Why?”

“Because you look happy.”

She looked at it. “Pengcheng? Do you think one day your mother will come and watch me? A premiere. An event. Something.”

He put his chopsticks down. “Would you want her to?”

“Yes. I want her to see what I do.”

“She might not understand it. She might not enjoy it.”

“That’s fine. It’s important to me.”

He understood, or thought he did. She wanted to be seen: not as the girl in the paper, or the guest at the New Year table, but standing on a stage holding something she’d worked for. She wanted his mother to understand that acting wasn’t a passing interest or an embarrassment. It was her work, and her life.

He reached across and took her hand. “Then perhaps she will.”

She kissed him, and leaned on his shoulder. “Next time I want you in the front row. Not three rows back. And I want you to clap louder.”

“I’ll try.”

“Promise?”

He turned his hand over and laced their fingers. “Next time, front row.”

She looked across at the lilies standing by the window: no card, no name, no word. She decided she’d keep them for tonight, because she wasn’t going to let an empty card hold the happiest evening of her life. She picked up the award and read the inscription again, and smiled to herself.

He kissed her temple. “Congratulations, Si-Yuan.”

“Thank you, Pengcheng.”

There was no audience to hide from now, and no camera, and no reason to keep any of it quiet. He took her hand, and stayed beside her until the lilies were the only things in the room still awake.

chapters.title: His Mother's Rules
chapters.desc: Eleven unwritten rules for his mother’s table, learned one dinner at a time. She stops wearing red. He notices everything about her except that.
chapters.content:
The first rule was that one never arrived empty-handed.

Si-Yuan learned it on a Sunday in April 2023, when his mother asked them to lunch. She spent forty minutes choosing a present, not because she enjoyed shopping for older women but because Madam Yang was impossible to buy for: she already owned everything she needed, disliked anything decorative, and preferred things that were expensive without looking it. In the end Si-Yuan chose a box of tea from a shop his aunt recommended, and wrapped it herself, and held it out with both hands on the step.

His mother took it. “You didn’t need to bring anything. Thank you.” Then, to her son: “Your father’s in the study.”

Si-Yuan didn’t know whether his mother liked the tea, or whether she’d chosen the right one. But she knew that next time she’d bring something. That was the first rule. She’d learn the other ten gradually, and none of them would ever be explained to her.

Two: one never arrives late. Seven means seven, whatever the traffic.
Three: one dresses appropriately. Not too casual, not too fashionable, not too young, and never as though one wanted to be looked at.
Four: one never interrupts an older person. Especially if the older person is wrong.
Five: one knows how to serve tea.
Six: one is never the first to leave the table.
Seven: one never talks about money unless asked.
Eight: one never talks too happily about one’s career.
Nine: one knows which relatives matter, which conversations need attention, and which remarks aren’t meant to be answered.
Ten: one never contradicts Madam Yang in front of other people.

The eleventh was the hardest. One should never make it obvious that one was trying. Si-Yuan didn’t learn that one until she’d broken it several times.

✦ ✦ ✦

By June she had a routine. She checked every invitation twice. She asked Pengcheng what the occasion was, who’d be there, and whether there was anything she ought to know. She kept a note in her phone. There was nothing in it she disliked or resented. It was information.

Mother: tea, no sugar.
Father: likes seafood.
Uncle Yang: arbitration, old court cases.
Auntie: orchids.
Nothing too colourful.
Don’t ask about the family’s business unless invited.
Greet Granduncle first.
Mother doesn’t like anyone arriving after the time on the card.

After a dinner in May she’d added one more line: Wear something simple.

She’d been to formal dinners all her life. She was an actress. She knew how to dress for an occasion, how to smile at strangers, how to answer questions without giving much away. But the Yangs were different. At work she could be herself. At their table she felt she was being measured against a standard nobody had ever shown her, and the measurements were never announced. They arrived as small corrections. That colour is bright. You’re holding the cup incorrectly. You should let the older guests begin. Perhaps something less conspicuous next time. None of it was loud, and none of it was openly cruel. It came in the same even voice his mother used for the weather, which made it impossible to answer. If Si-Yuan looked uncomfortable, she was oversensitive. If she replied, she was rude. If she said nothing, she was learning.

So she learned.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first time she wore red to a Yang dinner was in May, and she’d been happy about it. It was a dark red dress, not revealing in the least, with a plain neckline and sleeves that stopped just above the wrist, bought between two shoots because the colour made her feel brave. When Pengcheng looked up from his phone she turned in front of the mirror.

“New dress?”

“Yes. Too much?”

“No. It looks good. You’re beautiful in red.”

His mother arrived ten minutes after them and looked at the dress before she looked at anything else. “Red. Is there an occasion?”

Si-Yuan hesitated. “No, Madam. I just liked the colour.”

“I see,” said his mother, and turned to her son to ask about a matter in the southern district, and the talk moved on, and Si-Yuan sat down and looked at the red over her knees. It was dark, and plain, and hardly noticeable. But she remembered the look. In the cloakroom later she caught herself in the mirror, and the dress still looked lovely, and she straightened a sleeve and went back to the table. She never wore it to the Yangs’ again.

In August it was a silk blouse, a deep red, because she was meeting him straight from work and they were going directly to his parents’. She hadn’t thought about the colour until she was in his office.

“How do I look?”

“Good. Very good.”

At dinner his mother reached for her tea. “You’re wearing red again. It draws attention.”

Si-Yuan’s smile held. “I see.”

His mother turned to Pengcheng. “Your cousin’s engagement is next month. You’ll attend.”

“I’ll check my diary.”

“Don’t check. Make time.”

Si-Yuan ate when the others ate and smiled when she was spoken to, and that night she put the blouse in the note in her phone. She didn’t mean to wear it again. She wanted to remember.

✦ ✦ ✦

Pengcheng didn’t notice. He noticed other things. He noticed when she was worn out after a shoot, and when a headache made her quiet. He noticed when she stopped eating a dish because it upset her stomach. He knew her coffee and how much milk, that she hated her hair touched when she was working, that she liked the window seat, and that she’d steal the last piece off his plate if she thought he wasn’t looking. He was attentive in a hundred ways that made her feel loved.

He didn’t notice that she’d stopped wearing red. He only thought she’d been wearing more cream lately, and navy, and pale blue. He liked those on her. Once, when she came out of the bedroom in an ivory dress, he looked up from fastening his watch and said it suited her, and kissed her cheek, and asked if she was ready, and she was.

There were other adjustments, some too small for him to see. She stopped talking about filming at dinner unless someone asked, and stopped mentioning the harder parts of her work, after she heard his mother say that actresses were too easily influenced by the people around them. She learned to describe her schedule carefully. Instead of we worked till three, she said the production had been busy. Instead of I’m exhausted, she said she was managing. She learned that one aunt disliked being called by her first name, that one uncle expected people to stand when he came into a room, and that the old colleagues of the grandfather in the portrait were owed a particular kind of deference. She learned which stories could be told and which should stay home.

And she learned that his mother almost never gave instructions. She didn’t need to. A pause was enough, or a glance at someone’s sleeve, or a remark about another woman’s manners, or a sentence that began In our family. Si-Yuan understood, and adjusted, and next time did better.

✦ ✦ ✦

One evening in September he found her on the floor of his bedroom with three dresses round her: navy, pale beige, cream.

“What’s wrong with those?”

“Nothing. Which one’s better?”

He picked up the navy. “This.”

“Why?”

“It looks good on you.” He put it down beside her. “We’ll leave at six. Don’t spend too long deciding.”

He went back to the study. She looked at the three dresses, and picked up the navy one.

The dinner was at a private club, the older Yangs and several family friends. She arrived at six minutes to seven in the navy dress with her hair tied back and small pearls in her ears.

“You’re on time,” said his mother.

“Yes, Madam.”

She bowed to the older guests and remembered their names and asked after their health. She was careful not to say too much. When tea came she waited until the older women had been served. When the food came she served his mother first.

“Thank you,” said Madam Yang.

It was a good evening, or one of the better ones, until a family friend asked about her acting.

“I’ve seen you on television. You’re very popular now. Are you still filming?”

“Yes. A contemporary drama next month. The lead.”

“Very good. You’re young. Enjoy it while you can.”

His mother put her chopsticks down. “Acting is a demanding profession. It can be difficult to keep a stable schedule. Especially for someone who means to marry into a family like ours.”

“Well, that’s true,” said the family friend, with a small laugh.

Si-Yuan didn’t answer. His mother turned to her son about his father’s plans for him next year, and the talk moved on, and Si-Yuan picked up her tea, and put the cup down again so carefully it made no sound at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car he loosened his tie. “You’re quiet.”

“I’m tired.”

He took her hand across the console. “Long day? Did you eat enough?”

“Yes.” She looked at their hands. “Do you think your mother likes me more now?”

He thought about it. “She hasn’t said anything negative recently. She thanked you for the tea. And she said your dress suited you.”

Si-Yuan looked down at the navy. “She did.”

“See?”

She looked out of the window. She wanted to tell him she’d chosen the dress because she was afraid of choosing wrong. That she’d arrived six minutes early because she’d been frightened of being late. That she’d rehearsed his relatives’ names in the lift. That she’d stopped wearing red. It all seemed too small to say. It was only a dress, only a colour, and he was holding her hand. So she smiled, and said nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

By October she was good at the dinners. She knew when to speak and when to pour tea and when to laugh and when only to listen. She knew how long to stay, which relatives expected a goodbye, that his mother preferred presents brought in person, and that a compliment wasn’t an invitation to say more. She knew that when his mother said You must be busy, the right answer wasn’t her schedule. It was Not too busy, Madam.

She’d learned all eleven rules. She’d never written them down. She didn’t need to any more. They’d become reflex.

One Saturday they went shopping: a shirt for him, a present for Si-Jie’s birthday. In the department store she slowed in front of a dress near the entrance, a deep wine-red, with a soft drape and a narrow waist that caught the light when she moved.

“Do you like it? Try it.”

She laughed. “No. I don’t need it.”

“It would look good on you.”

“Maybe,” she said, and he tugged her hand gently, come on, your sister’s present, and she went, and neither of them looked back.

That evening, unpacking clothes she’d brought from her flat, she found a red blouse at the bottom of her bag. It was one of her favourites, the one she’d worn to the August dinner, still in good condition. She held it, and folded it, and put it at the very bottom of a drawer.

“You’re not wearing that?” he said from the doorway.

“I don’t feel like it.”

He touched her shoulder on his way past. “All right. Dinner’s ready.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the next family dinner she wore pale blue, because it was simple and suitable and unlikely to draw anybody’s eye.

“That colour suits you,” said his mother.

“Thank you, Madam.”

For the first time all evening she felt almost comfortable. Then a cousin’s wife arrived in bright red, and his mother said, “What a lovely colour. Very festive,” and the woman said her husband had chosen it.

Si-Yuan looked down at her pale blue sleeves. She didn’t know why it stayed with her. Perhaps because she’d spent months not wearing a colour another woman was now being praised for. Perhaps because she remembered the first red dress, and him saying she was beautiful in it, and that she’d never worn it again. She picked up her tea, and drank.

That night, in bed, he was reading a document and she was taking off her earrings.

“Mother seemed pleased. She said the blue suited you. You’re getting on.”

Si-Yuan lay down against him and listened to his heart. “Yes. Do you remember the red dress? In May. The first dinner.”

“The dark red one. Yes.”

“Do you remember what you said?”

“That you’re beautiful in red.”

She shut her eyes. He’d said it so plainly, and for a second she was back in front of his mirror in May. She wondered if she could wear red again. Just for him, and nowhere near his mother’s house. She didn’t say it. She moved closer, and he put his arm round her, and turned out the lamp.

✦ ✦ ✦

A week later he came home with a small paper bag. Inside were earrings: small, simple, a deep red stone set in gold.

“You looked at them in the window on Saturday,” he said.

“They’re beautiful.”

He watched her hold one to her ear. “Good.”

She laughed. “You always say that.”

“It’s usually true.”

She put them on and looked in the mirror. A warm, deep red. Nothing loud about it. And the thought came before she could stop it, so naturally that she almost didn’t recognise it as a thought at all: would his mother approve?

She turned and looked at him. He’d already opened his laptop. She looked back at the mirror, and smiled at the woman in it, and kept them on.

He never learned the eleven rules. He never knew she checked the time before every dinner, or kept a list of his relatives’ preferences, or had stopped wearing red because his mother had once said it drew attention, or practised her answers in the car. He saw the effort and mistook it for ease. He thought she was settling in with his family. He thought the dinners were getting better. And because she never complained, he assumed there was nothing to complain about.

That night, under the blanket, he found her hand.

“Pengcheng? Do you think I’m doing all right? With your family.”

He ran his thumb over her knuckles. “You’re doing fine. Don’t worry so much.”

“Okay,” said Si-Yuan.

She lay awake a while after he’d gone to sleep, with his hand round hers and a pair of red earrings on the bedside table, and was glad he thought she was doing well, and glad he didn’t have to worry. She’d become good at being the kind of woman the Yangs could put up with. She hadn’t noticed when she stopped being the girl who wore red because she liked it, or when she began asking herself what his mother would think before she asked herself what she wanted. In the morning she put the earrings on again, and went to work, and was happy in them all day.

chapters.title: Two Years
chapters.desc: Their second anniversary, and he forgets until three in the morning. Convenience-store flowers, a cake that says Two years, and the first time he calls her Yuan-Yuan. Explicit, slow, and more words from him than ever.
chapters.content:
She checked her phone for the fourth time a little after eight, and there was nothing, and she put it face up on his dining table and looked at the food.

Two portions. A small cake from the bakery near his flat. A bottle of wine she’d bought three days ago and hidden at the back of his fridge behind the eggs, where he’d never look, because he only ever looked at the eggs.

It was Wednesday the third of January 2024. Her last scene had wrapped at five and she’d come straight back, showered, changed, and turned down the crew’s drinks for the end of the shooting week. She’d wanted the evening to herself. More exactly, she’d wanted it with him.

Two years. She remembered the date because she’d remembered it every year: the morning she’d first sat across a desk from Yang Pengcheng with forty pages of contract between them and decided he was the most boring man she’d ever met. She’d been wrong about a great deal since. He wasn’t boring. He was careful with words. He remembered the smallest things about the people he cared for. He could be funny when he wasn’t trying. When he was tired he fell asleep sitting up with a document on his knee and his pen still uncapped. She knew how he took his coffee and how he folded his shirts and how his face went when he was concentrating, and how he kissed her when he thought she was already asleep. She’d learned him. Apparently she was still learning.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Are you still at the office?

The answer came eleven minutes later.

Pengcheng: Yes. Something came up. Eat first. Don’t wait for me.

She typed something, and deleted it, and typed again.

Miss Yen (Page Seventeen): Okay. Don’t work too late.

The cake sat in its white box with the ribbon still tied. She’d asked the bakery to write two words on it, Two years, and nothing else. She hadn’t wanted anything elaborate. She’d only wanted him to come home, and see the cake, and remember.

She ate. She washed up. She put the cake in the fridge. She changed into her pyjamas and watched half an episode of something without understanding a minute of it. Just after midnight she looked at her phone again. Nothing. She didn’t send anything else. She didn’t want to remind him. That was the part she couldn’t quite explain to herself. She knew he was busy. She knew his work could swallow a night whole when a negotiation reached its last stage, and she’d never once expected him to walk away from it for a date on a calendar. But she’d expected him to remember. And if she had to tell him, it wouldn’t be the same thing.

She turned off the television. She lay down on his side of the bed, facing the door. When her phone lit up after one she grabbed it, and it was the production group chat, and she put it down again, and some time after that she fell asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

He remembered at seven minutes past three. He was standing in a conference room on the twenty-first floor reading the final version of a settlement for the third time when his phone buzzed on the table, and the calendar put a line across the screen.

3 January. Si-Yuan.

For several seconds the words didn’t mean anything. Then he looked at the date, and the hand holding the phone went still.

“Mr. Yang? Shall I send this version across?”

“Give me ten minutes,” he said, and closed the file, and found that the settlement had gone out of his head entirely.

He remembered a desk and a pen. He remembered a girl in costume and plastic slippers looking at him over a bowl of noodles like she’d already decided he was worth teasing, and her mouth tasting of broth in his car, and her asking whether he liked her. He remembered the first night she’d fallen asleep in his flat, and how he’d stayed awake longer than he needed to because he hadn’t wanted to move. Two years. He’d forgotten.

Her last message was from before nine. Don’t work too late. He rang her. No answer. He rang again. He put the phone down and shut his eyes.

“Shit,” said Yang Pengcheng, under his breath, and the associate by the door pretended not to have heard.

✦ ✦ ✦

He left at half past three, still holding the phone, and in the lift he typed I’m coming home and didn’t send it, because she was asleep and it would only wake her. The roads were empty and wet. He stopped at a convenience store two streets from his flat and stood in front of the fridges for almost a minute: a small bouquet in cellophane, a box of chocolates, pastries in plastic. He couldn’t remember whether she liked white roses or pink. He remembered she’d once said she liked flowers that looked like they’d come out of a garden and not a shop. The cellophane bouquet looked like neither. It was the best there was at that hour. He bought it.

The flat was dark. The dining table had been cleared. When he opened the fridge for water he saw the white box through the glass shelf, and opened it, and on the cake, in neat dark icing, it said Two years.

He stood in his kitchen and looked at it. Then he put the flowers on the counter and went to the bedroom.

She was asleep on his side of the bed, one hand under her cheek, the other lying open on the empty sheet beside her. He’d seen her asleep hundreds of times. It was how ordinary it was that made it worse. He sat down on the edge of the mattress.

“Si-Yuan.”

She stirred. He touched her shoulder, and something else came out of him before he’d decided on it, a name he’d never once said aloud.

“Yuan-Yuan.”

Her eyes opened slowly. For a second she looked at him without knowing him, and then blinked. “Pengcheng? What time is it? You’re home.” She pushed herself up. “Did you eat? I’ll heat something—”

“Don’t get up.” He took her hand. “I’m sorry.”

She looked at his face, and at the clock, and understood before he said it. Something in her face went slightly still. “Oh.”

“I forgot. Today. I didn’t realise until the calendar told me.”

“It’s okay.”

“It isn’t.”

She looked at him. He almost never contradicted her when she was trying to make something easier for him. Tonight he did.

“It’s not about the date.” She stopped, and tried again. “I thought you’d remember.”

There was no accusation in it at all, and that was what made it hurt.

He lifted her hand and put his mouth against her knuckles. “I should have.”

Her eyes went to the doorway. “Did you bring flowers?”

“From the convenience store.”

A small laugh got out of her. “At three in the morning? Pengcheng. That’s very romantic.”

“You’re laughing at me.”

“A little.” Then, lower: “You called me Yuan-Yuan.”

“Yes.”

“You’ve never called me that.”

He looked down at their hands. “I know.”

She didn’t say anything. She reached for his sleeve and pulled, and he came, and she put her arms round his neck and held on. For a second he stayed stiff in her arms, not sure he was allowed the comfort. Then he held her back.

“Don’t say it’s all right just so I won’t feel bad.”

“I wasn’t.” She took his face in her hands. “I was disappointed. I waited. I wanted to celebrate with you, and I was sad when you didn’t remember. But I’m not going to stay cross with you for ever.”

“I wouldn’t expect you to.”

“Good,” said Si-Yuan, and kissed him, and didn’t tell him again that it was all right.

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t go back to sleep. She sat against the headboard with the blanket round her while he took his watch off and put it on the bedside table, tie loose, shirt still buttoned, hair out of place.

“Did you finish your work?”

“Almost.”

“Then why did you come home?”

“Because I remembered.”

“At three in the morning. After I was asleep.” She laughed under her breath. “You’re very bad at this, Pengcheng.”

“Next year I’ll remember.”

“That’s a long time away. Maybe we should celebrate this one first.” She looked at him. “Come to bed properly.”

He took his tie off. “Is that an invitation?”

“Don’t make me say it twice.”

He kissed her slowly. It wasn’t the absent kiss he gave her on his way to work, or the one he pressed to her temple going past her chair. It was deliberate. He held her face and waited until she turned into it, and her fingers went into his hair, and when he drew back she watched him.

“What?”

“I’m looking at you.”

“That’s what staring means.”

He undid his shirt and she pushed it off his shoulders, and he lifted her pyjama top over her head and looked at her in the grey light from the window the way he had the very first time, like there’d be an examination. He laid her down. He kissed her throat and her collarbone and her breasts, slow and certain, and down over her ribs, and she said his name once, low, and he lifted his head.

“I want to make tonight better,” he said.

“You don’t have to fix everything.”

“I know.” He kissed the inside of her hip. “I want you to know I love you without having to be told.”

She went still under his hands. It was the closest he’d ever come to saying it. She put her hand on his head and held it there, and he drew her pyjamas down her legs and put his mouth on her, and took his time, the way he always did, learning again things he already knew: where she wanted him, when she wanted more, when to slow. She came with her hand fisted in the sheet and her other hand in his hair and his name broken in half in her mouth, and pulled him up to her before she’d stopped shaking.

“Now. Please. Pengcheng.”

He came into her slowly and stayed there, his forehead on hers, and didn’t move until she moved first. Then they moved together, slow, the city dark beyond the window and the clock going on towards morning, and when she whispered his name he answered it, every time, I’m here, which was more words than he’d ever said to her in bed in two years. She held him through it. He finished with his face in her neck and her arms locked round his back, and lay on her afterwards heavy and breathing, and she stroked the back of his head and didn’t let him move.

“Are you still feeling guilty?” she said, a long time later.

“Yes.”

“That’s all right. I’m not angry any more.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me for forgiving you,” said Si-Yuan, and he made a small helpless sound that was nearly a laugh.

She traced his collarbone. “Do you know what I wanted today? Nothing expensive. I wanted you to come home, and remember before I had to tell you. And I wanted to eat the cake with you.”

“We’ll eat it tomorrow.”

“Breakfast cake?”

“Yes.”

She laughed into his chest. He kissed her hair.

“Happy anniversary, Yuan-Yuan.”

She shut her eyes and didn’t answer, and he thought she’d gone to sleep. Then she said, against his chest, “Nobody’s called me that since I was six. My grandmother. In Taipei. She used to shout it down the stairs when the dumplings were ready.”

He was quiet. “Shall I stop?”

“No. Keep it. It’s yours now,” said Si-Yuan, and she fell asleep before he could answer, and he lay awake a while longer saying it to himself in the dark, under his breath, getting it right.

✦ ✦ ✦

His phone went at a quarter past seven and he silenced it without opening his eyes.

“You’ve got work.”

“Five minutes.”

“You always say five minutes.”

“Today I mean it.”

“You’re a lawyer. You shouldn’t make promises you can’t keep.”

He opened one eye. “That’s unfair.”

He got up and went to make breakfast, and a minute later she heard the fridge open, and a pause, and his voice. “Did you buy this cake?”

He was in the bedroom doorway with the white box in his hands, looking at the two words on top, and then at her.

“Happy anniversary, Pengcheng,” she said.

He came back to the bed and put the box down and bent and kissed her. This time she hadn’t had to wait for him to remember.

They ate cake for breakfast. He cut two uneven slices, because he was no good at all with a cake knife, and she complained about the shape of hers and stole the bigger piece off his plate, and he let her. She took a photograph: no faces, only the two plates, the cellophane flowers in a glass in the background, and his watch beside her cup. She didn’t post it. She sent it to herself. At the other end of her gallery, two years back, there was a photograph of a bowl of beef noodles on a plastic table under a red awning. She looked at both of them.

He reached across and wiped cream off the corner of her mouth with his thumb. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“Next year I’ll take you somewhere. Anywhere you want.”

“That’s a dangerous promise.”

“I’ll manage.”

He took her hand, and held it while he drank his coffee, and didn’t let go even when his phone went again.

chapters.title: The Engagement Nobody Announces
chapters.desc: He proposes in his kitchen with a ring he’s kept for eleven days. His mother says wait, and he doesn’t argue. Her sisters see the ring at once. By September it spends its nights in a drawer.
chapters.epigraph: “Just make sure you’re not the only one waiting.”
chapters.content:
The ring was in his desk drawer for eleven days before he asked her.

He bought it on a Thursday in April 2024, because a hearing finished early and he walked back to chambers past a jeweller’s window. He hadn’t planned to buy it that day. He’d been thinking about it for months. She’d never asked him for a timeline or a promise. Once, watching a wedding in a drama on his sofa, she’d said she wanted a small one.

“How small?”

“Just the people we love.”

“And who would they be?”

“You’re asking me for a guest list?”

“I’m asking a question.”

“Then ask it properly,” she’d said, and he’d kissed her instead, and she’d laughed against his mouth and never brought it up again. He’d remembered. He’d also noticed how she looked at rings whenever they passed a jeweller’s. She never stopped, or pointed, or said anything. She only looked, and he’d begun to suspect she was trying hard not to make him feel pushed.

So he went in. He turned down the first two the woman showed him as too elaborate, the third as impractical, and the fourth because the stone was so large it would catch on her costumes. He chose a single diamond on a fine band, something she could wear every day. It looked like her. He took it back to chambers and put it in his desk drawer, because he wanted to ask properly.

✦ ✦ ✦

Properly turned out to be a Sunday evening eleven days later, in his kitchen.

She’d finished filming early and was in one of his shirts, cross-legged on the sofa, reading a script with a pencil behind her ear. He’d made dinner, fish and greens and soup, and she’d spent twenty minutes telling him about a scene she couldn’t crack, and he’d offered an interpretation she’d disagreed with, and she’d called him annoyingly logical, and he’d said it wasn’t the first time. Now she was reading again, and he stood in the kitchen doorway and watched her.

“Si-Yuan.”

“Mm?”

“Will you come here a minute.”

“Why?”

“Just come.”

She put the script down and came, and he took her hand, and for the first time that evening she saw something different in his face. He took the box out of his pocket. He didn’t kneel. He held it between them.

“I’ve been thinking about this for a while.”

She looked at the box, and at him. “About what?”

“Don’t make me explain the obvious.”

A laugh got out of her, unsteady. “Open it.”

He did. The diamond caught the kitchen light, and she went still.

“I want to marry you,” he said. He’d rehearsed several versions, and now that she was standing in front of him none of them seemed necessary. “I know we’re not in a hurry. I know your work matters to you. I’m not asking you to change anything. I want you to keep acting. I want you to have your own work and your own ambitions and your own choices. I want us to build something without either of us having to turn into someone else. And I want to come home to you, not because we’re used to it, but because I chose you.” His thumb moved over her knuckles. “So. Yuan-Yuan. Will you marry me?”

She looked at him like she was trying to keep the moment in her head exactly as it was. Then she laughed, breathless. “You’re asking me?”

“Is there someone else I should be asking?”

She hit his arm. And then she nodded. “Yes. Yes, I want to marry you.”

He slid the ring onto her finger. It fitted. She held her hand up under the light and turned it.

“How long have you had it?”

“Eleven days.”

“Eleven days? You could have told me.”

“Then it wouldn’t have been a surprise.”

She put her arms round him and pressed her face into his shoulder, and he felt her laugh turn into something softer against his shirt.

“I’m going to be your wife,” she said into it.

“Yes.”

She pulled back and looked at him, waiting, and he understood what she was waiting for without being asked, and said it.

“You’re going to be my wife.”

She smiled, and he kissed her, and for a little while there was nothing complicated about the future at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told his parents the following week. He didn’t ask their permission. He was twenty-seven, a lawyer with a practice of his own inside the chambers and a career that no longer hung on his father’s approval. He told them because it was the proper thing to do. His father congratulated him. His mother didn’t.

She sat at the head of the dining table and listened until he’d finished, and put her cup down. “Have you thought this through? Marriage isn’t something one decides because a relationship has lasted a few years. Your career is at an important stage. The family has expectations.” She paused. “And the girl?”

“Her name is Si-Yuan.”

“I know her name.”

“Then please use it.”

His father looked up.

His mother didn’t raise her voice. “She is young. She is an actress. Her career is unpredictable and her life is public. You know that better than anyone. Do you think that suitable for this family?”

He put his chopsticks down. “I think she’s suitable for me.”

His mother looked at him a long while. Then she said the thing that made the room go cold.

“At least wait. Until the next stage of your career. Until the family has settled its present matters. Until she has had time to think about what marrying you would actually mean.”

“She has thought about it.”

“Then she can wait. A marriage like this affects more than two people.”

He knew what she meant: the name, the chambers, the old friendships and obligations that came with them. He’d grown up hearing that a marriage was never only a private matter. He’d never thought it meant his mother should decide when he could have one.

“Mother. I’m not asking you to approve of every part of her career. I’m telling you I’ve chosen her.”

“And I am telling you not to rush.” She lifted her tea. “Wait a little longer. There’s no need to announce anything.”

He looked at his father. His father didn’t say a word. And the conversation was over: not because he’d agreed, but because his mother had decided she’d said enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told Si-Yuan two days later, over dinner at his flat. She’d been talking about a new script, and her face lit up when he said he’d spoken to his parents.

“What did they say?”

“My father congratulated us.”

“And your mother?”

He paused. “She thinks we should wait. Until things are settled. Work. The chambers. Some matters with my father. There’s no need to rush.”

She lowered her chopsticks. He didn’t look troubled. That was the first thing she noticed. The second was that he’d already accepted the word wait as a reasonable answer.

“Do you want to wait?”

“I want to marry you.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

He thought about it. “I don’t think a few months will make a difference.”

She turned the ring on her finger. “And if she still wants us to wait after that?”

He didn’t answer straight away. “Then we’ll discuss it.”

“All right,” said Si-Yuan.

He reached across the table and took her hand. “Don’t worry.”

“I’m not worried.”

She wanted to ask whether he’d told his mother he wasn’t going to wait. Whether he’d said he’d already asked, and that this was something the two of them had decided together. She didn’t. She asked instead whether he’d told his father about the ring, and he said no, he’d wanted her to be the first to know, and she said that was sweet, and smiled, and the conversation stopped there.

✦ ✦ ✦

One month went by, and then another. There was no announcement. No engagement dinner, no family photograph, no date. The ring stayed on her finger, and only the people nearest her knew what it meant. Her sisters knew at once.

“YOU’RE ENGAGED?” said Si-Jie, at a volume that made the café turn round.

Si-Yuan clapped a hand over her mouth. “Shh.”

Si-Wei put her drink down and took Si-Yuan’s left hand and looked at the ring. “When?”

“Last month.”

“And you’re telling us now?” Si-Jie sat back, delighted and outraged at once. “Where’s the announcement? Where are the flowers? Where’s the dinner? Where’s my future brother-in-law?”

“There isn’t an announcement yet.”

Si-Jie’s face changed. “Why not?”

Si-Yuan looked at Si-Wei, and back. “His mother wants us to wait. Family matters.”

“And what does Pengcheng think?”

“That there’s no need to rush.”

“Rushing isn’t the question,” said Si-Jie.

Si-Wei was still holding her hand. “Does he want to wait?”

Si-Yuan smiled. “He wants to marry me.”

“That isn’t what I asked either,” said Si-Wei.

For a moment nobody said anything. Then Si-Yuan laughed. “You’re both making it sound worse than it is.”

Si-Jie reached over and took her other hand. “We’re happy for you. Really happy. But I don’t want you to feel you have to earn the right to wear it.”

Si-Wei let go of her hand at last. “Just make sure you’re not the only one waiting.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t tell her to take it off. He didn’t ask her to hide it. He just didn’t announce it. She wore it to family dinners, and his mother noticed, because his mother noticed everything, and never once mentioned it. In May, while Si-Yuan was pouring her tea, his mother glanced at her hand.

“That’s a new ring.”

“Yes, Madam.”

“It suits your hand,” said his mother, and turned to another guest, and that was all. No congratulations. No question. No sign that her son had asked a woman to be his wife. Si-Yuan went on pouring. Pengcheng was beside his father talking about a case, and didn’t see it happen.

In June, in bed, she asked whether they should choose a date. She’d been scrolling through wedding venues on her phone, showing him the odd one she liked, while he read a legal opinion.

“Not yet. After things settle down.”

“How long will that take?”

He put the document aside. “I’m not sure.”

“Neither am I,” she said, and smiled, and he took her hand.

“I haven’t changed my mind, Yuan-Yuan. I want to marry you.”

“I know.” She did know. That was the hard part. “I know you do.”

He seemed relieved, and kissed her, and she let herself sink into the familiarity of him, and when he drew back he put his forehead to hers and told her not to think too much, and she said all right.

✦ ✦ ✦

By July the ring had become part of her. She took it off only when a costume required it. In interviews she turned the stone inwards when the cameras came close. It was an engagement ring that nobody outside a small circle knew was one, and the longer it went unannounced, the more it felt like something she was carrying on her own.

In August his mother asked them to dinner. Si-Yuan wore soft grey, arrived on time, brought a present, greeted every older relative in the right order, and sat beside him. Everything was as it should be until the dessert, when his mother laid her spoon down.

“Pengcheng. Have you considered the matter we discussed? Your engagement. I think it better not to announce anything yet.”

Si-Yuan’s fingers tightened on her napkin.

“Why?”

“There are matters to settle. Family matters.”

“Be specific.”

His father looked up. His mother’s voice cooled by a degree. “Your father’s partnership discussions are continuing. The family has commitments. It would be inappropriate to put another large event into the calendar.”

“Our marriage isn’t a scheduling inconvenience.”

“Nobody said it was.”

“Then why are we delaying it?”

“Because there are things you don’t yet understand.”

“I understand perfectly well.”

“Then behave as though you do,” said his mother, and the room went quiet.

His jaw moved. Under the table Si-Yuan touched his wrist, the smallest movement, and when he glanced at her she shook her head so slightly nobody else could have seen it: not here, not tonight. She knew the rules. He looked back at his mother, and after a moment picked up his cup.

“We’ll discuss it another time.”

His mother went on eating, and the talk moved on, and Si-Yuan kept her fingers on his wrist a few seconds longer, and then took them away.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car he was silent for several minutes. Then: “You shouldn’t have to deal with that.”

“She’s your mother.”

“That doesn’t make it acceptable.”

For a moment she felt something warm and hopeful. Then he went on: “We’ll wait until things settle down.” And the hope went back to wherever it lived.

“All right.”

He took her hand. A streetlight caught the diamond. “Does it bother you? Waiting?”

She thought about telling him the truth: that she didn’t mind waiting if they were waiting together; that a quiet engagement was fine if it was only for now; that she could bear his family’s doubts if he’d only make it plain the decision was still theirs.

“Not if we’re both waiting,” she said.

“We are.”

“Okay,” said Si-Yuan, and he kissed the back of her hand, and she let him.

That night in his bed he moved her hair off her cheek. “Are you upset?”

“I’m tired.”

“You know I want this. I didn’t ask you so I could leave you waiting.”

“I know.”

He kissed her again, slower, like he could persuade her that the words he hadn’t said to his mother didn’t matter, and his hand found her waist, and for a while she let herself forget the dining room and the silence and the careful phrasing. There was only him, the warmth of him and his mouth and the way he held her, already his wife. When at last he drew back he put his forehead to hers, and said it into the dark, for the first time, so lightly it might have been anything.

“Love you.”

She smiled with her eyes shut. “Love you too.”

He’d said it at last, and he’d said it in the dark, and she lay awake a long time afterwards knowing he’d meant it, and that he’d never once said it in front of anyone at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

In September the ring went into a drawer. Not because she’d stopped wanting it. She had a part that needed her character unmarried, and wardrobe asked her to take off all her jewellery, and she put it in a small silk pouch, and that evening put the pouch in his bedside drawer, and in the morning she forgot to put it back on.

He noticed while he was reaching for his watch. “Where’s your ring?”

“Oh. In the drawer.”

He found the pouch and gave it to her, and watched her slide it on, and kissed her cheek. “Don’t lose it.”

“I won’t,” she said, and he went for his jacket, and she looked at the ring, and at the drawer, and shut the drawer. It was such a small thing. A piece of jewellery. A question that had already been answered.

By the end of the summer there’d been no announcement and no family meeting and no date, and no acknowledgement of any kind from the Yangs. But he still called her his future wife when they were alone. He still reached for her hand, and kissed her before he left for work, and talked about a future in which they lived together and travelled together and grew old together. And she still loved him. That was the difficult part. She didn’t doubt his love. She doubted what he was willing to do with it.

One evening she opened the bedside drawer looking for a hair tie and found the pouch there again, and was holding it in her palm when he came in.

“Is that the ring? Why aren’t you wearing it?”

“I was just looking at it.”

He took the pouch and the ring out of it, and took her left hand and slid it on, and turned her hand in the light. “Still beautiful.” He kissed the ring, and then her, slowly, tenderly, as though the kiss could stand in for the conversation they hadn’t finished, the date they hadn’t chosen, the announcement that hadn’t come. “One day soon,” he said.

She wanted to ask how soon. She kissed him again instead, and he smiled against her mouth, and she let him believe that was enough.

Later, when he was asleep, she got up for water, and on the way back stood in the doorway and looked at him: on his side, one arm stretched across her empty pillow. She got back into bed, and took the ring off, and put it in the drawer, and lay down beside him. In the morning she’d put it on again. She’d go to work, and smile for cameras, and sit beside him at another dinner, and be patient, and understanding, and never ask him to choose between her and his mother. And she’d go on waiting for the day he chose their marriage without asking anyone else to make room for it.

He reached for her in his sleep and found her hand under the blanket, and she laced her fingers into his, and lay still beside the man who’d asked her to be his wife, with the ring a few centimetres away in the drawer, waiting too.
